news.title: Anthropic releases FlashProve, open-source code that cryptographically verifies an AI response came from a given model, not a cheaper one swapped in by a router (Anthropic)
news.title_en: Anthropic releases FlashProve, open-source code that cryptographically verifies an AI response came from a given model, not a cheaper one swapped in by a router (Anthropic)
news.author: Anthropic
news.article_content:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:

The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.

Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.

Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?

The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:

These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.

Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.

Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.

Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.

Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. EZKL (2023) proved a 1M-parameter GPT-style transformer in about 966 s per token (≈0.001 tok/s). Performance progressively improved: zkLLM (2024) proved LLaMA-2-13B on a 2,048-token input in about 15 minutes on GPU, which is ≈0.001 tok/s per new token, or ~2.5 tok/s in the batch. In 2025, zkGPT reduced GPT-2 to 21.8 s (≈0.05 tok/s), zkPyTorch proved Llama-3 8B at ~150 s per token on one CPU core (≈0.007 tok/s), and ZKTorch proved GPT-J (6B) in about 20 minutes (≈0.001 tok/s). VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. DeepProve, a current peer-reviewed state of the art, certifies an entire generated sequence with a single forward pass. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100.

Recently commercial efforts have reached impressive numbers, with Attestable proving Gemma 4 31B at 53–77 tok/s on a single H100; at the time of writing, Attestable has not released a corresponding open source library.

news.original_content:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used. For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets. An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses. The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a cheaper one or a degraded version. In general, how can users verify that they are being served by their chosen model?

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements existing mechanisms for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

Regulation might require providers to serve only models approved as safe, rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that only approved models are served?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

A note on PI from trusted hardware. Prior work often focuses on trusted execution environments to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our technical report; here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases:

The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated.

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

We measured an implementation of the protocol on Llama 4 Maverick (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran vLLM, a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried.

Inside the system. The underlying mechanism behind FlashProve is a zkSNARK of the kind deployed in peer-to-peer systems (e.g., L2 networks such as Starknet or Mantle for blockchains like Ethereum). Our zkSNARK is built according to a well-established recipe: an underlying information-theoretic object called an interactive oracle proof (IOP) is compiled into a cryptographic proof by relying on hash functions (and offers even post-quantum security). Our IOP is assembled from state-of-the-art building blocks using tools such as code proximity tests with linear constraints and lookup arguments, which are based on techniques from coding theory and complexity theory. Combining these pieces into a bespoke IOP for inference is a delicate task; more details about the construction can be found in the technical report.

FlashProve benefits from architectural decisions that we took, and which are discussed in detail in the technical report. Here we highlight a few:

When integrating proving mechanisms into inference servers there is a choice: in-line proving (i.e. proving alongside the inference) versus post-hoc proving (i.e. proving after-the-fact, for a subset of tokens). Our system follows the latter. In-line solutions are expected to be ultra-fast and may sacrifice security for efficiency, whereas post-hoc solutions are allowed to be slower and may not suffer such a tradeoff. On the other hand, post-hoc proving has limitations: added complexity of recomputation, the delay in getting guarantees about your traffic, and inherent “non-determinism”. We elaborate on the motivation and implications of post-hoc proving in the technical report.

Cryptographic code is notoriously brittle and error-prone. How can users trust the code we’re releasing today?

The answer is formal verification: we use the Lean proof assistant to specify the protocol and the desired security properties. We prove these properties in a form that is machine-checkable and guaranteed to be correct (up to compiler errors). We target three top-level properties:

These properties are stated in the so-called random oracle model, an information-theoretic way to analyze cryptographic protocols that rely on hash functions.

Formal verification leaves two important trust gaps. First, the formal statements must be audited to ensure that they match their intent. This has to be done manually (though it is dramatically less onerous than auditing proofs); we provide an interactive visualizer to assist with this.

Second, the executable code must be audited to ensure it matches the formally-defined protocol for which the security properties are proven. How to best assist with this depends on the property, because soundness depends solely on the verifier, zero-knowledge depends solely on the prover, and completeness depends on their interaction.

Achieving provable inference is the objective of a line of work colloquially termed “zkML”. Early works, such as SafetyNets (2017) verified a two-conv-layer MNIST CNN and a small fully connected speech model, zkCNN (2021) reached VGG-16 (15M parameters) at 88.3 s per proof, and Kang et al. (2022) proved MobileNet v2 on full-resolution ImageNet.

Transformer proofs followed: ZKML’s GPT-2 took about 159 s per token for 117M parameters (≈0.006 tok/s), and Modulus Labs’ 1.5B-parameter GPT-2 XL needed over 90 hours. VerInf proved Llama 4 Maverick (the same 400B-parameter MoE model we prove) at ≈0.02 tok/s. It reaches about 2.9 tok/s for GPT-2 and 1.4 tok/s for Gemma 3 on one machine, and 31 tok/s distributed. SASH's prover (2026) reached ≈1.25 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B on a single H100.

news.article_content_zh:
罗伊·林伯格（人类）、亚历克斯·阿兰（人类）； Alessandro Chiesa（洛桑联邦理工学院、StarkWare）、Miranda Christ（麻省理工学院、RESI）、Rahul Dalal（人类 STEM 研究员计划，简明）、Giacomo Fenzi（洛桑联邦理工学院）、Ben Mayer（人类研究员计划，麻省理工学院）、Guy Weissenberg（洛桑联邦理工学院）

当您亲自与朋友交谈时，您可以通过多种方式知道那确实是他们：您可以看到他们、听到他们、与他们握手。当你与人工智能模型交谈时，你几乎什么也没有。今天查询模型的用户无法检查响应是否来自开发人员声称正在响应的特定模型，而不是出于成本原因被路由服务秘密替换的模型，甚至是被篡改令牌流的攻击者替换的模型。仅从模型的输出来看是不可靠的，即使它产生了高质量的响应。加密推理证明解决了这个问题：它们让模型提供者提交一个模型，然后证明每个响应都是由该模型生成的。此类证明可以支持从消费产品到内部安全的各种应用，并有助于构建用于验证是否符合人工智能节奏要求的工具包。

具体来说，我们在一种称为“zkSNARK”的强大加密证明方面取得了进展，它特别适合可证明的推理（由于其强大的隐藏性和效率特性）。在这篇文章中，我们主要通过我们称为 FlashProve 的系统分享了其中的一些进展。简要技术总结如下：

我们在 Apache 2.0 许可证下发布我们的代码、精益证明和文档。1 这篇研究文章旨在分享中间进展，而不是完整的研究议程。我们明确分享这一点的目的是让其他人看看我们所做的事情，接受并改进它。

当用户向人工智能模型发送请求时，他们现在无法确定他们选择的模型是否是生成响应的模型。对于日常使用，用户最关心的是输出，而不一定是哪个特定模型产生的，这是一个不太紧迫的问题。但在某些情况下，这种保证是有用的。例如，在发布之前和之后测试人工智能模型的独立评估者需要知道他们正在评估的模型是正在服务的模型。通过第三方路由服务使用模型的客户希望确保代币来自他们支付的模型。如果网络攻击者在冒充给定模型的同时修改了令牌流，则用户无法仅从输出中检测到它。

然而，验证模型响应具有挑战性。大多数前沿模型的权重都是保密的，即使用户可以访问权重，检查给定的响应是否是由具有这些权重的模型生成的也需要运行模型，这需要的计算资源远远超出了典型用户（甚至评估者）可以承受的范围。

可证明推理 (PI) 的目标是使计算资源有限且没有任何权重信息的用户能够验证响应是否来自所请求的模型。 PI 的动机不仅是希望增加客户对人工智能提供商的信任，而且因为它可以用来向独立评估者提供保证，并允许提供商证明他们正在履行某些承诺和法律义务，它还对人工智能开发前沿和人工智能监管产生影响。

实现 PI 的一种方法是通过称为零知识简洁参数的加密对象：模型提供者与声明的响应一起发送一个简短的证明（例如，几兆字节），用户可以快速验证（理想情况下，在 CPU 上只需几秒钟）。如果声称的响应偏离指定模型，则用户的检查将失败。重要的是，加密技术确保证明不会透露任何有关模型权重的信息。

今天，我们发布了 FlashProve：一个用于可证明推理的开源高性能原型。对于 400B 参数混合专家模型（Llama 4 Maverick，4 位量化），我们表明单个 H100 GPU 以超过 100 个令牌/秒的速度生成证明，每个 1,024 个令牌请求的证明大小约为 19 MB（大约是常见开源库 vLLM 处理相同长度提示所需的 GPU 时间的 70-95 倍）。

该版本附带可执行代码、精益形式化和协议的技术描述。我们的目标有两个：（i）加速和促进可证明推理的发展； (ii) 证明零知识简洁论证对于可证明的推理是实用的。

我们相信，这一进展对于安全、加快人工智能开发速度、为人工智能客户提供完整性保证、为审计员和监管机构提供工具等方面具有重要意义。

人工智能的发展及其在数字基础设施和经济中日益增长的作用提出了人工智能提供商必须应对的信任挑战。依靠可证明推理 (PI) 工具可以帮助解决这些和其他挑战。

PI 工具包括硬件方法、软件方法或两者的组合。在这里，我们专注于一种纯软件方法：一种称为“zkSNARK”（零知识简洁知识论证）的加密工具。非正式地说，zkSNARK 是一个系统，允许证明者通过简短的“证书”让验证者相信给定的计算已正确执行；至关重要的是，该证书是零知识的，因为它不会透露超出计算正确性所暗示的信息，而且它很简洁，因为与经过证明的计算相比，它的验证速度要快得多。

下面我们概述了几个挑战以及 zkSNARK 如何帮助解决这些挑战。

news.title: Apple opens Siri AI to all developers with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 OS betas, letting any app bring its content and actions into Siri AI by using App Intents (Apple Developer)
news.title_en: Apple opens Siri AI to all developers with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 OS betas, letting any app bring its content and actions into Siri AI by using App Intents (Apple Developer)
news.author: Apple Developer
news.article_content:
Starting today with the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas, a new Developer Preview enables any developer to integrate their app with Siri AI, giving businesses and developers new ways to reach and serve their customers.

Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that is profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal, is designed to be deeply integrated into Apple’s operating systems and the apps people use every day, including the apps from our vast ecosystem of developers. Thousands of developers have already built integrations with Siri to let users ask for directions, manage a to-do list, send a message, or catch up on an audiobook. Siri AI is available in many languages, including English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish and will soon expand to support Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese. People around the world are turning to Siri AI to get things done every day, which means more customers can discover and use apps just by asking.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience. And Siri AI can now surface any entity in the Spotlight semantic index, not just the ones that fit an existing schema.

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year. There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers. With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers. This preview provides early access before first shipping to customers in a few months; and with submission to the App Store opening up in the spring, developers have time to explore, build, and help shape their experiences before launch. Try it out and share your feedback.

As you explore early, we will follow up with more details about the terms and usage policies for experiences enabled through Siri AI. More to share soon.

To learn more about the new APIs, how to use them, and how to evaluate your app’s experience with Siri AI, read new documentation. You can also connect with Apple engineers in Apple Intelligence Group Labs on November 4–5 to ask questions, get advice, and follow the discussion.

news.article_content_zh:
从今天开始，从 iOS 27.3、iPadOS 27.3、macOS 27.3 和 VisionOS 27.3 Beta 版开始，新的开发者预览版使任何开发者都可以将其应用程序与 Siri AI 集成，为企业和开发者提供接触和服务客户​​的新方式。

Siri AI 是 Siri 的全新版本，功能更加强大、更具对话性和个性化，旨在深度集成到 Apple 的操作系统和人们每天使用的应用程序中，包括来自我们庞大的开发者生态系统的应用程序。成千上万的开发者已经与 Siri 建立了集成，让用户可以询问方向、管理待办事项列表、发送消息或收听有声读物。 Siri AI 支持多种语言，包括英语、法语、日语、韩语、葡萄牙语和西班牙语，并将很快扩展到支持繁体中文、挪威语、土耳其语和越南语。世界各地的人们每天都在求助于 Siri AI 来完成工作，这意味着更多的客户只需询问即可发现和使用应用程序。

今天的预览版允许任何应用程序通过使用应用程序意图将其内容和操作直接引入 Siri AI，从而使所有应用程序更轻松地利用 Siri AI 的最新功能，包括个人上下文理解、屏幕感知、自然语言等。因此，人们只需用自己的话寻求帮助，Siri AI 就会执行您构建的任何自定义操作，从检查送货到预订再到下订单。对于复杂的请求，我们还引入了一些技能，让您可以教 Siri AI 如何将多个操作组合成一个体验。 Siri AI 现在可以显示 Spotlight 语义索引中的任何实体，而不仅仅是适合现有模式的实体。

我们开始在许多 Apple 应用程序中推出这些新功能，包括日历、文件、Finder、日记、邮件、地图、消息、音乐、笔记、照片、预览、提醒、Safari、快捷方式和天气，以便用户可以执行诸如查找上周访问过的咖啡店或归档一年多没有打开的文件等操作。现在还有更多操作示例可供您参考。要了解每个应用程序可以执行哪些操作，只需询问 Siri AI。

此开发者测试版让开发者可以一睹 Siri AI 应用意图。借助此早期开发者预览版，您的应用程序可以直接与 Siri AI 配合使用，让您首先了解接触和服务客户​​的新方法。此预览版提供了在几个月后首次发货给客户之前的早期访问；随着春季开放的 App Store 提交，开发人员有时间在发布前探索、构建和帮助塑造他们的体验。尝试一下并分享您的反馈。

当您尽早探索时，我们将跟进有关通过 Siri AI 实现的体验的条款和使用政策的更多详细信息。更多内容即将分享。

要了解有关新 API、如何使用它们以及如何评估应用程序使用 Siri AI 的体验的更多信息，请阅读新文档。您还可以于 11 月 4 日至 5 日与 Apple Intelligence Group Labs 的 Apple 工程师联系，提出问题、获取建议并关注讨论。

news.title: Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds
news.title_en: Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Stanford researchers tested 50 widely cited claims about LLMs against 20 current models. 44 percent of the findings are already "expired," and another 34 percent have weakened significantly. The average lifespan is just 15.7 months. Claims about what models can't do expire fastest.

The article Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds appeared first on The Decoder.

news.summary_en: Stanford researchers analyzed 50 widely cited claims about LLMs, finding that 44% are obsolete and 34% have significantly weakened, with an average shelf life of just 15.7 months. ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 斯坦福研究人员对比分析了50项关于大语言模型的权威研究，发现约44%的结论已完全失效，34%的结论效力显著减弱，平均有效期仅为15.7个月。其中，关于“模型不能做什么”的论断失效速度最快，反映出AI技术的进化速度已彻底碾压了学术界对其进行解释和归纳的能力。

(Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.)

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: Steam平台近期审核效率大幅下降，导致开发者提交的构建版本长时间处于待审批状态。多家独立游戏工作室因错过既定的上线节点，被迫发布延期声明，这一瓶颈反映出平台在面对激增的游戏提交量时人工审核流程已不堪重负。

news.title: Netflix will show you themed recommendations through a new ‘AI Discover’ tab
news.title_en: Netflix will show you themed recommendations through a new ‘AI Discover’ tab
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
Netflix's TV app is getting a new "AI Discover" tab where the company will show experimental, AI-powered features to help you find new shows and movies to watch.

The first of these experiments surfaces content based around themes, like "Something Light," "Family Movie Night," or "Quick Watches." When you pick a theme, Netflix will show you recommendations that match it. If you don't like a recommendation, you can tell that to Netflix, and the app will remember it.

The company says that AI Discover is powered by "a new intelligence layer we've been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning."

news.title: Microsoft updates Windows 11 to make PCs with 8GB of RAM up to 20% more responsive and multitasking up to 40% faster in lab tests, utilizing memory compression (Lance Whitney/ZDNET)
news.title_en: Microsoft updates Windows 11 to make PCs with 8GB of RAM up to 20% more responsive and multitasking up to 40% faster in lab tests, utilizing memory compression (Lance Whitney/ZDNET)
news.author: ZDNET
news.article_content:
The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

news.article_content_zh:
Windows 11 的最新更新在速度、性能和内存管理方面进行了改进。

Windows PC 的内存越多，执行速度就越快，尤其是在处理多个应用程序、文件和其他数据时。我的笔记本电脑有 32GB 内存，而我的台式机有 64GB 内存，两者都非常快。这是否意味着内存只有 8GB 甚至更少的计算机都是失败者？不，根据微软的说法，不是。

另外：您的电脑真正需要多少内存？

在周二发布的一篇新博客文章中，微软宣传了最新更新在 Windows 11 中实现的速度、性能和内存管理方面的进步。这些对 RAM 仅有 8GB 的​​ PC 的影响尤为明显，这些 PC 现在可以比以前更快、更高效地运行多个应用程序和文件。

为了实现这一目标，该公司表示有三个想法。

首先是更好地利用每台 Windows 11 PC 上的现有内存。第二个是保护需要感觉即时的任务，即使使用更多内存也是如此。第三是确保关键应用程序和 Windows 需要更少的内存。是的，具有 16GB、32GB 或 64GB RAM 的计算机可以更好地处理更密集的活动。但微软希望确保 8GB 系统也能跟上步伐。

根据其自己对 8GB RAM 电脑的实验室测试，该公司声称 Windows 现在比最新更新之前的响应速度提高了 20%，多任务处理速度提高了 40%。方法如下。

随着分配更多内存，Windows 必须将不活动的应用程序和文件从 RAM 移动到硬盘驱动器。当您需要再次访问这些应用程序和文件时，您必须等待 Windows 将它们从磁盘存储移回 RAM。通常，内存较少的电脑必须进行大量的磁盘交换。

Windows 减轻此过程痛苦的一种方法是通过压缩。在这里，操作系统将不太活跃的数据缩小为较小的格式，以便它可以保留在内存中。尽管 Windows 已使用压缩多年，但 Microsoft 已对该技术进行了微调，以确定压缩程度、何时将数据从 RAM 移动到驱动器以及何时取回数据，尤其是在具有 8GB 内存的 PC 上。

微软表示，因此，Windows 现在可以在内存中保留最多 2GB 的活动数据，而不是将其移动到存储中。当您返回打开的非活动应用程序、文件或浏览器时，不太可能需要从硬盘驱动器重新加载。

打开“开始”菜单、启动文件资源管理器、右键单击文件夹或文件以及搜索项目都是需要即时完成的任务；否则，Windows 本身就会感觉迟缓。微软表示，为了在 RAM 较少的 PC 上实现这一目标，Windows 会尝试优先考虑需要完成的某些操作，同时放弃搜索索引等后台任务。

这是一个例子。更新计算机并重新启动后，Windows 需要执行一些内务处理工作。但发生的任何设置工作都不应影响打开应用程序或文件所需的时间。

据微软称，与 2026 年 1 月的版本相比，最新版本的 Windows 11 将此类任务和交互的速度提高了 20%。

然而，多任务处理对只有 8GB RAM 的 PC 造成的压力最大。为了分析这一点，微软表示，它在同一台 8GB 内存的 PC 上进行了两次测试。一项测试测量了 Windows 11 的当前版本，而另一项测试则测量了 2026 年 1 月的版本。测试人员在 Microsoft Edge 中打开了 20 个选项卡，开始播放 4K 视频，并在 Word、PowerPoint 和 Excel 中依次启动大文件。该公司表示，当前版本的 Windows 比其前身快 40%。

news.title: Rockstar plans to let users pre-load GTA VI on November 10, ahead of its November 19 launch, and says the game requires up to 212GB "depending on your device" (Emma Roth/The Verge)
news.title_en: Rockstar plans to let users pre-load GTA VI on November 10, ahead of its November 19 launch, and says the game requires up to 212GB "depending on your device" (Emma Roth/The Verge)
news.author: The Verge
news.article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rockstar says to make sure you have ‘ample space’ on your device.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

You’re going to need a lot of extra storage space on your console if you’re planning to play Grand Theft Auto VI later this month. Rockstar Games confirmed on Tuesday that the pre-load file will require up to 212GB “depending on your device.”

Rockstar says you can start pre-loading the game on the PlayStation 5 on Tuesday, November 10th at midnight in your local time zone, while users on Xbox Series X | S devices can start pre-loading on November 10th at 12AM GMT. The company says to “make sure you’ve got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible.” Rockstar also posted a support page with more information about pre-loading the game.

The announcement lines up with recent rumors suggesting that the game could take up a significant amount of storage space. GTA VI launches on November 19th for $79.99 and is only available via digital download. Physical versions of the game will include just a code in the box.

news.title: AI agents take over at SETI's Allen Telescope Array, scanning for extraterrestrial intelligence
news.title_en: AI agents take over at SETI's Allen Telescope Array, scanning for extraterrestrial intelligence
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
The SETI Institute and Breakthrough Listen are now using AI agents at the Allen Telescope Array to control the telescope and analyze incoming radio signals. Tasks that used to take weeks can now wrap up in hours, and the team says the system detected a pulsar in the Crab Nebula in real time for the first time.

news.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
news.title_en: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational.

Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim?

2023年，被追踪为BlackLotus的恶意软件成为第一个公开记录的UEFI引导套件，能够在完全更新的Windows 11系统上绕过安全引导。随着整个行业的信任链机制被破坏，恶意软件能够在Windows完全加载之前运行恶意代码，许多安全防御措施也开始运作。

微软已经在 2022 年修复了 BlackLotus 利用的漏洞。在 2023 年和 2024 年，微软发布了额外的更新。第一个添加了一个不再信任易受攻击的启动管理器的新证书。第二个提供了撤销对用于签署较旧的易受攻击的 Windows 启动管理器的数字证书的信任的方法。被新 bootkit 感染的组织（以 BlackX 的名称进行追踪）已经安装了所有这些补丁。那么他们是如何成为受害者的呢？

news.title: Binance says North Korean hackers stole $6.3B through a months-long scheme with fake LinkedIn job interviews and an ad campaign to deliver malicious software (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
news.title_en: Binance says North Korean hackers stole $6.3B through a months-long scheme with fake LinkedIn job interviews and an ad campaign to deliver malicious software (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
Binance on Tuesday disclosed that North Korean hackers used a mix of social engineering and malicious software to pull off last week’s $6.3 billion heist, the biggest in crypto history. Speaking to reporters, company executives revealed that the hackers targeted a Binance engineer on LinkedIn and arranged a series of fake job interviews in order to persuade the employee to download an “assignment” that let them invade the company’s systems.

In a related report, Binance explained that: “Software Engineer B was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform by an individual posing as a Project Director. Software Engineer B had a profile on the platform that referenced his experience at Binance. The purported Project Director arranged a first-round interview with a HR representative, followed by a second-round interview with an individual claiming to be the CEO of a fictitious company.”

The report also provided additional details about the sophisticated months-long scheme that involved not only the fake LinkedIn recruitment, but also used a separate ad campaign that tricked another engineer into downloading a malicious version of a popular software package called Homebrew.

According to Binance, the engineer in question did not download the Homebrew software though the company’s regular channels, but instead clicked on an internet ad promoting a tampered version of it.

Binance says it detected the fake Homebrew download and removed it from the employee’s machine, but not before the hackers discovered critical information about the engineer’s role and others who managed the company’s wallets.

It was the combination of these exploits—the fake LinkedIn outreach and the knowledge gleaned from the tampered Homebrew download—that allowed the North Korean hackers to take over a series of Binance wallets and drain them of funds.

While many initially speculated that the hackers had used AI to break into Binance, the company’s account shows how they instead relied primarily on conventional phishing tactics. At the same time, Binance added that AI did play a role. This occurred when the hackers, after gaining control of the engineer’s laptop, used Binance’s own internal AI tools to compromise other accounts.“The attacker leveraged the compromised computer of engineer B and used an internal AI tool to gain control over the Wallet DevOps Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C. The attacker soon discovered Wallet DevOps Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer,” stated the Binance report.

According to a Binance spokesperson, employees with non-public facing roles are not allowed to maintain LinkedIn profiles. The spokesperson declined to explain if the engineer in question had violated that policy, or if either of the engineers would be terminated.

The phenomenon of North Korean hackers posing as recruiters has become a widespread problem across the corporate sector more broadly. In the case of Binance, the company said it flagged earlier efforts by hackers to target its employees on LinkedIn and that, in 2026, had detected and prevented 57 North Korea-related hacking attempts.

Since the attack, which occurred over several hours on Thursday, the company has disclosed that the hackers stole around $6.3 billion, but that it was able to recover around $2.5 billion of that after two companies, Tether and Circle, moved to freeze stolen stablecoins.

In response to the hack, Binance shut down withdrawals for around 48 hours, but re-enabled them on Saturday. The company has repeatedly stated that all customer funds are safe, and has replenished 98% of the stolen coins from reserve funds and other sources. It is in the process of acquiring the remaining 2%, which consist of lesser used currencies.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” said Binance in a statement.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

news.article_content_zh:
币安周二透露，朝鲜黑客利用社交工程和恶意软件的结合，上周完成了加密货币历史上最大的 63 亿美元盗窃案。公司高管在接受记者采访时透露，黑客针对 LinkedIn 上的一名币安工程师，安排了一系列虚假的工作面试，以说服该员工下载“任务”，从而入侵公司的系统。

币安在相关报告中解释道：“一名冒充项目总监的个人通过合法的求职平台联系了软件工程师 B。软件工程师 B 在该平台上有一份个人资料，其中提到了他在币安的经历。这位所谓的项目总监安排了与人力资源代表的第一轮面试，随后又安排了与自称是一家虚构公司首席执行官的个人的第二轮面试。”

该报告还提供了有关长达数月的复杂计划的更多细节，该计划不仅涉及虚假的 LinkedIn 招聘，还使用了单独的广告活动来欺骗另一名工程师下载名为 Homebrew 的流行软件包的恶意版本。

据币安称，该工程师并未通过该公司的常规渠道下载 Homebrew 软件，而是点击了宣传该软件被篡改版本的互联网广告。

币安表示，它检测到了虚假的 Homebrew 下载并将其从员工的计算机中删除，但在此之前，黑客发现了有关工程师角色和管理公司钱包的其他人的关键信息。

正是这些漏洞的结合——虚假的 LinkedIn 外展活动和从被篡改的 Homebrew 下载中收集的信息——使得朝鲜黑客能够接管一系列币安钱包并盗取其中的资金。

虽然许多人最初猜测黑客使用人工智能闯入币安，但该公司的账户显示他们主要依赖传统的网络钓鱼策略。同时，币安补充称，人工智能确实发挥了作用。当黑客在控制了工程师的笔记本电脑后，使用币安自己的内部人工智能工具来入侵其他帐户时，就发生了这种情况。“攻击者利用工程师 B 受感染的计算机，并使用内部人工智能工具来控制钱包 DevOps 工程师 A 和另一名钱包软件工程师 C。攻击者很快发现钱包 DevOps 工程师 A 在其计算机上拥有容器部署权限令牌，”币安报告称。

据币安发言人称，担任非公开角色的员工不得维护 LinkedIn 个人资料。该发言人拒绝解释相关工程师是否违反了该政策，或者其中任何一名工程师是否会被解雇。

朝鲜黑客冒充招聘人员的现象已成为整个企业界的一个普遍问题。就币安而言，该公司表示，其早先在 LinkedIn 上标记了黑客针对其员工的行为，并于 2026 年检测并阻止了 57 起与朝鲜相关的黑客企图。

自周四发生的几个小时的攻击以来，该公司披露黑客窃取了约 63 亿美元，但在 Tether 和 Circle 两家公司采取行动冻结被盗的稳定币后，该公司能够追回约 25 亿美元。

为了应对此次黑客攻击，币安关闭了提款功能约 48 小时，但于周六重新启用。该公司多次表示所有客户资金都是安全的，并已从储备金和其他来源补充了98%的被盗币。它正在收购剩余的 2%，其中包括较少使用的货币。

币安在一份声明中表示：“这种情况不应该发生，对于它给我们的用户、合作伙伴和更广泛的行业带来的担忧、干扰和不确定性，我们深表歉意。”

杰夫·约翰·罗伯茨 (Jeff John Roberts) 是《财富》杂志的金融和加密货币编辑，负责监督区块链的报道以及技术如何改变金融。

news.title: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
news.title_en: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
The 2026 midterm elections will determine the scope of President Donald Trump’s power in his final two years in office, and signal what voters care about going into the 2028 presidential election. While this year’s races are expected to be most broadly defined by affordability issues, there’s several topics impacting the tech industry that appear to be on voters’ minds.

Among them are concerns about data centers, and whether voters will have to bear the burden of higher energy costs, AI safety, and the rapid expansion of surveillance technology through Flock. There’s also the question of how to tax billionaires’ wealth in California, a topic that has driven heavy tech spending and creative stock class structures meant to keep tech executives from fleeing the state should a ballot measure pass.

The next Congress is likely to continue grappling with how to regulate AI, and stem the data center backlash, among other issues. How that conversation shapes up, and which tech CEOs are hauled to testify on Capitol Hill, will be shaped by the outcome of November 3rd.

news.title: ChatGPT Consumer Product Lead Adam Fry says ChatGPT has hit 1.2B WAUs, adding 200M over the past two months, and its search volume is now ~20% of Google's (Alex Kantrowitz/Big Technology)
news.title_en: ChatGPT Consumer Product Lead Adam Fry says ChatGPT has hit 1.2B WAUs, adding 200M over the past two months, and its search volume is now ~20% of Google's (Alex Kantrowitz/Big Technology)
news.author: Big Technology
news.article_content:
OpenAI says ChatGPT growth is accelerating.

The company added 200 million users over just the past two months, jumping from 1 billion to 1.2 billion weekly active users in 60 days. Its search volume, it says, is approximately 20% of Google’s. Its users create 1.5 billion images with it per week. And its voice mode, between dictation and speaking with ChatGPT, now has 250 million combined weekly active users.

ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry told me this during a brief fireside chat at an OpenAI-hosted dinner in New York City on Monday night. “The growth is just going big,” he said.

During our conversation, Fry also revealed plans to merge ChatGPT’s Chat and Work modes (so that confusing toggle up top will soon go away), agreed with feedback that ChatGPT-created restaurant signage looks too uniform, and addressed the cost to serve its personal assistant Dots.

Here’s a look at our full conversation, lightly edited for clarity and length. We also cover image generation, interactive interfaces, advertising, education, and public unease about AI:

Alex Kantrowitz: OpenAI has analyzed ChatGPT’s search volume and compared it with Google’s. What did you find?

Adam Fry: ChatGPT has been growing quite quickly. ChatGPT’s volume of search-like queries is now roughly one-fifth the volume of queries of Google.

It’s a pretty amazing statistic when you think about it, mainly because we started just about a year and a half ago. It’s hard to remember this, but ChatGPT at a time didn’t have any up-to-date information. You’d ask a question, it would say something like, “It’s past my training date,” and nobody had any idea what that meant.

You’re saying ChatGPT’s search volume is one-fifth of Google’s. Bing’s share of the search market is around 5%. Does that make you multiple times larger than Bing?

To say that more directly, ChatGPT has gone from one billion to 1.2 in just the last two months. That’s roughly 100 million users in 30 days, and another 100 million in another 30 days. The growth is just going big, and we’re staying very focused on how fast ChatGPT is growing.

What counts as a search? I might have 20 prompts back and forth in a ChatGPT conversation. Does each one count as a query?

Moving upmarket means saying yes to what enterprise buyers ask for first: SSO, directory sync, and audit logs. WorkOS gives you all three, so your team keeps building the product instead of the checklist.

Adam Fry: What people came to ChatGPT for to start, if you go back about two years, is really writing help and coding help. Those wouldn’t be things that you really search for.

What we’ve seen over the last year is people have grown into all these other topics. Things like you’re looking up a person or people or a place or a thing, and it requires up-to-date information. That’s a key element.

Another big part is finance questions or health questions, where you really want to make sure it’s up-to-date information that’s quite factual, and we’ll do a web search for those questions.

It’s basically anything that a user would have traditionally gone to a traditional search engine for, but is now deciding to go to ChatGPT for.

Does each conversation with a search embedded count as one search, or does every question that requires a web search count?

Every time you ask a question and go search the web, that’s a search.

You used to work at Google. How would you say the nature of search is changing?

One of the things that people really love about ChatGPT is this personalization and this understanding of the broader journey.

If you look in the past, people would go for a Q&A box, and you’d ask a one-off question, like how tall is the Eiffel Tower. But there’s so much context in our lives around, “Maybe I’m taking a trip to Paris.”

It’s actually helpful for ChatGPT to respond, “Here’s how tall the Eiffel Tower is, but I know you’re going on a trip to Paris.” It’s that ability for people to actually maintain context over time that has led them to start using ChatGPT in this way.

You’ve also announced 250 million weekly active users of voice input, including dictation and conversations with voice mode.

We are at 250 million weekly active users. What’s amazing about this is, if you look at those 250 million, what we’re seeing is it’s actually also incremental to the product.

It’s no longer just a novelty. People aren’t just trying out voice. We’re seeing them use voice input day to day in their daily life, and it’s grown so quickly.

Those 250 million users are using voice input, and that could just be a quick question or a long conversation. We’re seeing both behaviors. We’re seeing people just not want to type. You just hold it and start talking to it, or it turns into a longer conversation where people just sit with it.

The big reason for this is the frontier capabilities of our models that we’ve shipped. We shipped what we call GPT Live 1, and then we shipped GPT Live 1.1. The big change with this is that it’s much more natural to speak with.

It’s something we call backchanneling and interruptibility.

What you just did there is what the model does, because it’s really good at having a bidirectional conversation. That push to the frontier—we were the first to really release this at scale—has made it so much more natural for people to chat.

That’s still only about 20% of the user base. From the outside, that looks small. Why is it exciting from the inside?

It’s very exciting for a few reasons. We see from the data that when people start using voice, they stay around using voice.

One of the things, transparently, we can do a better job of is bringing more people into discovering it. We see that the number of people who discover it could be a lot higher. But once they do, it’s a really new way for people to interact with AI.

We’ve made a lot of improvements to it too, where we’re just going to see the number go up. You have background mode, so now by default, if you close the app, it’ll show, “Hey, the conversation’s still going.”

Dots launched on September 29 and is about a month old. How’s it doing?

You’re more conservative with permissions than some competitors. I tried to give my Dot my credit card, and it wouldn’t take it. With the creator of OpenClaw in-house, why are Dots’ permissions more limited?

We’ve just talked about how you go to this 1.2 billion user growth and asking questions. Now we’re asking people, “Can you ask ChatGPT or your Dot to help get things done?” But when you ask it to help get things done, it’s a whole new level of trust.

We’ve built up a tremendous amount of trust in giving the right answers to your questions, and we want to make sure that when we build this new product, it has a high degree of trust.

It’s a long game. We think this is going to be a new market for a very long time, and we want to make sure that we’re being this trusted player in the market to start.

I initially thought Dots would be available on my $20 plan, then realized I had to spend $100 a month to get it. I upgraded, but I’d like to downgrade at some point….

We hope to keep earning your business and make the value good enough.

It’s a really good point. ChatGPT’s goal more broadly, which I think is unique for us in the market, is we are focused on bringing intelligence to everyone safely across the entire world. For Dots in particular, there’s no difference.

We don’t have anything to share tonight about the date of when Dots will go to a broader set of users. But you can rest assured we’re working very hard, and there are a couple things we have to get right.

Over time we’re going to work on more efficient, agentic models that are able and capable of doing things for you.

The first one is, right now we wanted to make sure that your Dot is actually really helpful. We started with some of our best models, but over time we’re going to work on more efficient, agentic models that are able and capable of doing things for you.

The second thing is around proactivity. We’re still dialing in: How much do I message you to help you get things done? We can always play around with that to understand how much usage should a user use to have a successful Dot.

We’re going to work on both, and our goal and ambition is to bring it out to all users.

This is our premium, always-on personal assistant. Once we nail that, we’ll figure out how to dial back the compute needs.

On ChatGPT and on our consumer business, we’ve been extremely proud of our ability to diversify different revenue streams in a way that’s growing really fast.

On ads, within 200 days, we reached more than a billion in ARR, and that business is growing extremely quickly.

One thing we continue to bet on at OpenAI and ChatGPT more broadly is that the models will continue to get much better and much cheaper, way faster than any of us think.

If you look back at the historicals on it, it continues to be true. From what I’ve seen, I see no slowing down of that.

One of the things they’ve done well is this simplicity. You just go in and you can ask a question. You don’t have to think too much about what you’re doing. That’s one thing that seems to have resonated with users, which we also believe in.

Second, there’s something really nice about being able to access your agent across many different channels. We just announced and launched Dots on iMessage.

Whether you talk to your Dot on email or iMessage or within the ChatGPT app, the ubiquity in getting your assistant out there is going to be key. Those are two things that, if I had to be nice to our competitors, I would say were two big ones.

So Alexandr Wang’s meme-tweeting strategy isn’t something you’re going to emulate?

ChatGPT still asks me to choose between Chat and Work, even though some people call this technology AGI. Will that distinction go away?

It’s solvable. There’s real research to solve to make sure the models can understand what your intent is. Are you asking for a fast, quick reply? Are you asking me to go do a long agentic task?

We’re going to solve it, and the plan is to bring Chat and Work together.

So one interface will work out whether I’m asking for a conversation or a task. When?

You told me the majority of ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users are using image functionality. What are they doing?

Today, 1.5 billion images are created per week. It’s hard to even wrap my head around that number. They’re doing a wide range of things.

One of the most interesting things they’ve started to do is really use it for productivity use cases.

The first thing it started with—I don’t know if you saw the ’80s trend, but it was quite fun. You could take a photo of yourself and say, “Put me and my family in ’80s outfits.” I did this for my family, and it was a really fun poster.

I agree with the feedback, and we’ll take it to the team.

As you go to the extreme, what you can imagine is, let’s say you’re using voice mode, and you just say, “Show me how offside works.” Immediately it should show you a visual diagram, and you say, “No, I don’t quite understand it.” It should just repopulate.

That’s where the future of this technology goes. It’s almost like you’re talking to a canvas that will update and change.

People are finding it helpful for a lot of things. My favorite one is—it’s hard to admit that I had no idea how hearts work. The last biology course I took was in high school. I just asked it, “How does the heart work?” and it instantly gave me a beautiful interactive diagram of where blood flows and how it goes through.

I’m really, really bullish on this for learning in particular.

You’ve described useful applications in finance, health, and learning, and ChatGPT has 1.2 billion users. If people are getting so much value, why is public polling on AI so negative?

The reality with AI is it is going to change the nature of how work gets done. For a lot of people, that is something that can feel scary at times, and we’ve all felt that.

But I remain confident that when people actually use the product and they use AI, it very quickly changes how they perceive it. We’re at 1.2 billion, but there are still a lot of people who haven’t used it.

The more people use it, get familiar with it, how it can actually help you in your life, it’s going to feel a lot less scary.

news.article_content_zh:
OpenAI 表示 ChatGPT 的增长正在加速。

仅仅过去两个月，该公司就增加了 2 亿用户，60 天内每周活跃用户从 10 亿跃升至 12 亿。据称，其搜索量约为 Google 的 20%。它的用户每周用它创建 15 亿张图像。它的语音模式（介于听写和与 ChatGPT 交谈之间）目前每周活跃用户总数达到 2.5 亿。

周一晚上，ChatGPT 消费产品负责人 Adam Fry 在 OpenAI 于纽约举办的晚宴上进行简短的炉边聊天时告诉了我这一点。 “增长正在变得越来越大，”他说。

在我们的谈话中，Fry 还透露了合并 ChatGPT 的聊天和工作模式的计划（这样令人困惑的顶部切换很快就会消失），同意 ChatGPT 创建的餐厅标牌看起来过于统一的反馈，并解决了为其个人助理 Dots 提供服务的成本问题。

以下是我们的完整对话，为了清晰和长度而进行了轻微编辑。我们还涵盖图像生成、交互界面、广告、教育以及公众对人工智能的不安：

Alex Kantrowitz：OpenAI 分析了 ChatGPT 的搜索量，并将其与 Google 进行了比较。你发现了什么？

Adam Fry：ChatGPT 发展得相当快。 ChatGPT 的类似搜索查询量现在大约是 Google 查询量的五分之一。

仔细想想，这是一个非常惊人的统计数据，主要是因为我们大约一年半前才开始。很难记住这一点，但 ChatGPT 当时没有任何最新信息。你问一个问题，它会说“已经过了我的训练日期”，但没有人知道这意味着什么。

你是说 ChatGPT 的搜索量是 Google 的五分之一。 Bing 在搜索市场的份额约为 5%。这会让你比 Bing 规模大好几倍吗？

更直接地说，ChatGPT 在短短两个月内就从 10 亿增长到了 1.2。这意味着 30 天内大约有 1 亿用户，再过 30 天又增加 1 亿。增长速度很快，我们非常关注 ChatGPT 的增长速度。

什么算搜索？我可能会在 ChatGPT 对话中来回出现 20 个提示。每一个都算作一个查询吗？

进军高端市场意味着满足企业买家首先提出的要求：SSO、目录同步和审核日志。 WorkOS 为您提供了这三个功能，因此您的团队可以继续构建产品而不是清单。

Adam Fry：如果回溯到大约两年前，人们来到 ChatGPT 的目的实际上是编写帮助和编码帮助。这些并不是你真正寻找的东西。

去年我们看到人们已经开始关注所有这些其他话题。比如您正在查找一个人或多个人、一个地方或一件事，它需要最新的信息。这是一个关键要素。

【起因与机理】为了向外界展示生成式AI产品爆发式增长的商业势能与技术渗透率
【关键数据与实测】ChatGPT周活跃用户在两月内大增至12亿，产品增长持续加速。
【观点态度】官方计划近期简化产品界面，取消令人困惑的Chat和Work模式切换。

[Key Metrics] Search volume hits 20% of Google's, voice mode reaches 250 million WAUs.
[Perspective & Impact] Company plans to simplify UI by merging Chat and Work modes.
