items.title: this is f*cking insane. andrej karpathy: "the biggest regret of every engineer in my field right now is every AI convers
items.title_en:
this is f*cking insane. andrej karpathy: "the biggest regret of every engineer in my field right now is every AI conversation they never saved, and in 10 years the ones who started saving in 2024 will be running circles around the rest of us"

andrej karpathy, co-founder of openai, pulled 16M views on one idea: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain that remembers every article, pdf, transcript and conversation you ever fed it

you point claude code at a folder, drop anything into it, and claude reads it, cross-links it with everything already there, and writes it into a living wiki. your knowledge finally compounds instead of leaking out of your head every friday

the stack:

→ brew install obsidian, mkdir ~/vault, cd ~/vault
→ run claude in that folder and type "init a knowledge vault with CLAUDE.md as the rules, /raw for sources, /wiki for your pages"
→ drop any file into /raw (youtube transcript, meeting notes, 400-page pdf, screenshot of a tweet) and type "ingest"
→ claude writes a wiki page, links it to 5 existing ones automatically, updates CLAUDE.md with any new pattern it noticed about how you think
→ never open a blank claude chat again. every question goes through the vault, every answer cites your own sources with dates and links

5 minutes to set up. compounding knowledge from that evening forward

the ugly part most will scroll past: in 10 years the engineers who started this in 2024 will remember every book, every podcast, every meeting with receipts. you will remember none of them. karpathy already picked which side he is on and you are still not on his

full step-by-step is in the article below

bookmark this before you waste another monday

openai 联合创始人 andrej karpathy 的一个想法获得了 1600 万次浏览：停止使用人工智能编写代码，用它来构建第二个大脑，记住你曾经喂给它的每一篇文章、pdf、文字记录和对话

andrej karpathy, co-founder of openai, pulled 16M views on one idea: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain that remembers every article, pdf, transcript and conversation you ever fed it

you point claude code at a folder, drop anything into it, and claude reads it, cross-links it with everything already there, and writes it into a living wiki. your knowledge finally compounds instead of leaking out of your head every friday

5 minutes to set up. compounding knowledge from that evening forward

the ugly part most will scroll past: in 10 years the engineers who started this in 2024 will remember every book, every podcast, every meeting with receipts. you will remember none of them. karpathy already picked which side he is on and you are still not on his

items.title_en:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!

I copied the video clips from my DJI to a folder, then opened Claude Code in it and asked it to edit it into a 10 minute vlog

I made a few adjustments but not a lot

It transcribed everything I said with mlx-whisper (Whisper large-v3-turbo running on my MacBook Pro's GPU through Apple's MLX)

It pulled video frames every few seconds into grid images (contact sheets), so Claude could see what's in each clip

It used SpeechBrain ECAPA (a voice-matching model) to figure out what was my voice from other people

It then made thumbnails with OpenCV with YuNet's face detector

The edit itself is a list of cuts in a JSON file: which clip, start time, end time, Claude then picked the pieces by reading the transcripts and looking at the frame grids by itself

I added on screen captions for X and on YouTube for the first minute with Pillow (Python's image library)

P.S. I didn't ask for any of this, and I didn't know any of this until @thesamparr just asked me how I edited it

All I asked for was "Claude can you edit these clips into a 10 minute vlog for X and YouTube"

I think if I didn't have AI to edit it, I wouldn't be vlogging because editing would be such a painful and slow process for me and hiring someone to do it would be even more hassle for me!

items.quote_zh:
我今天的视频博客完全由 Claude Code 使用 Opus 5.5 编辑！

我将视频片段从 DJI 复制到一个文件夹，然后在其中打开 Claude Code 并要求它将其编辑成 10 分钟的视频博客

我做了一些调整，但调整不多

它转录了我用 mlx-whisper 所说的一切（Whisper large-v3-turbo 通过 Apple 的 MLX 在我的 MacBook Pro 的 GPU 上运行）

它每隔几秒钟将视频帧拉入网格图像（接触表），这样克劳德就可以看到每个剪辑中的内容

它使用 SpeechBrain ECAPA（一种语音匹配模型）来找出我从其他人那里听到的声音

然后使用 OpenCV 和 YuNet 的人脸检测器制作缩略图

编辑本身是 JSON 文件中的剪辑列表：哪个剪辑、开始时间、结束时间，然后 Claude 通过阅读脚本并自行查看帧网格来挑选片段

我使用 Pillow（Python 的图像库）在 X 的屏幕标题和 YouTube 上添加了第一分钟的标题

附：我没有要求任何这些，我也不知道这些，直到 @thesamparr 只是问我如何编辑它

我所要求的只是“克劳德，你能将这些剪辑编辑成 X 和 YouTube 的 10 分钟视频博客吗”

我想如果我没有人工智能来编辑它，我就不会做视频博客，因为编辑对我来说是一个痛苦而缓慢的过程，而且雇人来做这对我来说会更麻烦！

items.title: A look at VC-backed glossy magazine Colossus, whose glowing profiles of Zuckerberg and other tech titans win industry praise, while Kara Swisher says it is PR (Andrew Fedorov/The San Francisco Standard)
items.title_en: A look at VC-backed glossy magazine Colossus, whose glowing profiles of Zuckerberg and other tech titans win industry praise, while Kara Swisher says it is PR (Andrew Fedorov/The San Francisco Standard)
items.author: The San Francisco Standard
items.article_content:
A venture capitalist’s glossy quarterly wants to be The New Yorker for tech billionaires.

Many media veterans doubt the profiles accomplish their subjects’ public relations goals. “It’s all well and good for the tech industry media bubble to have its own in-flight magazine, but audiences aren’t stupid,” Nilay Patel, editor-in-chief of The Verge, said in an email. “Writing a massive profile of Mark Zuckerberg in which … his staggering unpopularity with everyday Americans is treated as an unfortunate byproduct of his ambition just isn’t going to convince anyone of anything.

“If Mark actually wanted to be understood as he says he does, he’d sit down for a truly adversarial journalistic interview and try to make his case,” Patel added. “But I don’t think he can take the risk.”

Colossus is the brainchild of Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a Connecticut-raised heir to an oil fortune, who went to work for his father James’ firm, O’Shaughnessy Asset Management, in 2007. Patrick took over the company in 2018 and sold it four years later to Franklin Templeton. In 2016, he launched a podcast called “Invest Like the Best,” borrowing the title of a book his father published in 1994.

His guests on the podcast have included Berkshire Hathaway Vice Chairman Charlie Munger and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In 2020, building on the success of “Invest Like the Best,” which O’Shaughnessy has said gets north of 100,000 downloads per episode, he launched a podcast network called Colossus, which now has shows like “Business Breakdowns” and “Founders.” The same year, he spun up a venture capital firm, Positive Sum.

“It’s actually great that venture capitalists are now writing all of the founder hagiography, because it means that when, inevitably, one of these people goes to prison, the blowback will not affect mainstream journalists,” said Casey Newton, founder of Platformer and cohost of the new NPR podcast, “Machine Gods.” “It will just affect the venture class, and they can take it.”

But Colossus is the first in this wave of VC-sponsored media to make a serious effort to ape the writing and photography of glossy magazines. “This kind of wet kiss has always existed, but it was never done this artfully,” said Samtani. “To be super clear, it is not journalism. It is positioned, oftentimes, as journalism. They hire journalists, but it is not journalism. Think of it as high-grade, tier-one content marketing.”

The upside is less for the magazine itself, Samtani explained, than for O’Shaughnessy’s venture firm. “Their economics are not media company economics. This is at least partly a clout exercise and an access game, and it’s a very smart one,” he said. “Media is an incredible way to create connections and develop your own influence.”

Notably, O’Shaughnessy failed to absorb the first paragraph of Remnick’s introduction, which establishes the form’s ethos. He wrote that The New Yorker’s founding editor, Harold Ross, “prized intimacy and wit over biographical completeness or, God forbid, unabashed hero worship. Ross told his writers and editors that, above all, he wanted to get away from what he was reading in the other magazines — all the ‘Horatio Alger’ stuff.”

The typical Colossus profile follows the classic Alger trajectory: scrappy kid overcomes adversity to achieve success. But Colossus adds a twist befitting our nepo-baby era. Its subjects tend to be born not in rags but with relative riches. Their great accomplishment is to accumulate even more money than their well-off parents.

To fit Kushner’s story to the Alger narrative, Stern spans three generations to his beloved grandmother Rae, who survived the Holocaust. He glosses over the less savory parts of the Kushner family history — among them, his father Charles hiring a prostitute to entrap his brother-in-law.

With Zuckerberg, the Colossus editor focuses on Mark’s father’s quaint dentist office and both parents’ authentic New York accents, spelling out their pronunciation. He skips mentioning Phillips Exeter, the elite prep school that polished Zuckerberg’s Latin and nurtured his sense of imperial destiny.

The secondary sources are routinely impressive. The Kushner profile includes comments from Altman, Demis Hassabis, Jony Ive, John Collison, and the former dean of Harvard Business School. But it’s rare to find independent perspectives; almost everyone quoted by name has a financial relationship with the subject. And few of Colossus’ sources ever criticize or question the motivations of the subject.

In the magazine’s pages, we’re invited to understand and relate to these wounded colossi, vulnerable hulks persevering on the path to greatness through a nearly insurmountable accumulation of wounds. (Think of St. Sebastian, beatific with all the arrows in him.) Stern praises Kushner’s “mostly vindicated admirers” and castigates his “increasingly sheepish critics.” Zuckerberg’s detractors suffer from “Zuckerberg Derangement Syndrome,” persecuting “the most persistent scapegoat of the 21st century.”

When journalists talk about Stern and his Colossus colleagues, you sometimes hear traces of pity. They know what the marketplace for magazine journalism looks like today — there are few paying customers for profiles that actually delve into the darker corners of celebrity businesspeople’s psyches. “I’m sure that there is some desire by the writers writing these pieces to go further than the actual piece goes,” said Samtani.

In interviews, Stern occasionally expresses mild revulsion toward technology investors. “I had always found the personality types kind of annoying,” he told Meservey. “As a class of people, these people feel like they’re full of shit.” Yet such sentiments are rarely reflected in his work in the magazine.

Other practitioners suspect Colossus writers are simply wasting their time. Zuckerberg and oligarchs of his ilk, Newton said, make for bad interviews because “most important information about them is already public. You’ve seen the products. You’ve seen what they do to people. You’ve seen the fact that the company will often try to evade making [its products] safer or reckon[ing] with its role in society.”

Newton questions the value of trying to understand or analyze their interior lives. “Against that backdrop, what kind of kid was Mark Zuckerberg? It’s like, who fucking cares?” he said. “I’m sorry. It doesn’t matter.”

items.article_content_zh:
一家风险投资家的光鲜季刊希望成为科技亿万富翁的《纽约客》。

许多媒体资深人士怀疑这些资料能否实现他们的主题的公共关系目标。 “科技行业媒体泡沫拥有自己的机上杂志固然很好，但观众并不傻，”The Verge 主编尼莱·帕特尔 (Nilay Patel) 在一封电子邮件中表示。 “写一篇关于马克·扎克伯格的巨著，其中……他在普通美国人中极不受欢迎，被视为他的野心的不幸副产品，这不会让任何人相信任何事情。

帕特尔补充道：“如果马克真的希望像他所说的那样被理解，他会坐下来接受真正对抗性的新闻采访，并试图阐明自己的观点。” “但我认为他不能冒这个险。”

Colossus 是帕特里克·奥肖内西 (Patrick O’Shaughnessy) 的创意，帕特里克·奥肖内西 (Patrick O’Shaughnessy) 是一位在康涅狄格州长大的石油财富继承人，他于 2007 年前往父亲詹姆斯的奥肖内西资产管理公司 (O’Shaughnessy Asset Management) 工作。帕特里克 (Patrick) 于 2018 年接管了该公司，四年后将其出售给富兰克林邓普顿 (Franklin Templeton)。 2016 年，他推出了一个名为“Invest Like the Best”的播客，借用了他父亲 1994 年出版的一本书的书名。

他在播客上的嘉宾包括伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司副主席查理·芒格和 OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼。 2020 年，奥肖内西称《Invest Like the Best》每集下载量超过 10 万次，在其成功的基础上，他推出了一个名为 Colossus 的播客网络，该网络现在有《Business Breakdowns》和《Founders》等节目。同年，他创办了一家风险投资公司正和。

Platformer 创始人兼新 NPR 播客“机器之神”联合主持人凯西·牛顿 (Casey Newton) 表示：“风险投资家现在正在撰写所有创始人的传记，这实际上是件好事，因为这意味着，当其中一个人不可避免地入狱时，主流记者不会受到影响。” “这只会影响风险投资阶层，他们可以接受。”

但 Colossus 是这波风险投资赞助媒体中第一个认真模仿光鲜杂志的写作和摄影的媒体。 “这种湿吻一直存在，但从来没有做得这么巧妙，”萨姆塔尼说。 “要非常明确的是，这不是新闻业。它通常被定位为新闻业。他们雇用记者，但它不是新闻业。将其视为高级的一级内容营销。”

萨姆塔尼解释说，对杂志本身来说，好处不如对奥肖内西的风险投资公司来说。 “他们的经济学不是媒体公司的经济学。这至少在一定程度上是一种影响力练习和一种获取游戏，而且这是一个非常聪明的游戏，”他说。 “媒体是建立联系和发展自己影响力的一种令人难以置信的方式。”

值得注意的是，奥肖内西未能理解雷姆尼克引言的第一段，该段确立了该形式的精神。他写道，《纽约客》的创始编辑哈罗德·罗斯“看重亲密和智慧，而不是传记的完整性，或者，上帝禁止，毫不掩饰的英雄崇拜。罗斯告诉他的作家和编辑，最重要的是，他想摆脱他在其他杂志上读到的东西——所有‘霍雷肖·阿尔杰’的东西。”

典型的巨像形象遵循经典的阿尔杰轨迹：斗志旺盛的孩子克服逆境取得成功。但 Colossus 增加了一个适合我们的新生儿时代的转折。它的主题往往不是出生时衣衫褴褛，而是相对富裕。他们的伟大成就是比他们富裕的父母积累了更多的钱。

为了使库什纳的故事与阿尔杰的叙述相吻合，斯特恩跨越了三代人，直到他深爱的祖母雷伊（Rae）在大屠杀中幸存下来。他掩盖了库什纳家族历史中不那么令人愉快的部分——其中包括他的父亲查尔斯雇佣妓女诱骗他的姐夫。

与扎克伯格一起，Colossus 编辑重点介绍了马克父亲古色古香的牙医诊所和父母双方地道的纽约口音，并拼出了他们的发音。他没有提及菲利普斯埃克塞特大学，这所精英预科学校曾打磨扎克伯格的拉丁语并培养了他的帝国命运感。

二手资料通常令人印象深刻。库什纳的简介包括奥特曼、德米斯·哈萨比斯、乔尼·艾维、约翰·科里森和哈佛商学院前院长的评论。但很少能找到独立的观点；几乎每个被引用名字的人都与该主题有经济关系。 Colossus 的消息来源很少批评或质疑该主题的动机。

在该杂志的页面中，我们被邀请去理解和理解这些受伤的巨人，脆弱的巨人，通过几乎无法克服的伤口积累，坚持走上伟大的道路。 （想想圣塞巴斯蒂安，他身上满是箭。）斯特恩称赞库什纳的“大多数都是平反的崇拜者”，并严厉斥责他“越来越羞怯的批评者”。扎克伯格的批评者患有“扎克伯格精神错乱综合症”，他们迫害“21世纪最持久的替罪羊”。

当记者谈论斯特恩和他的巨像同事时，有时你会听到一丝怜悯。他们知道当今杂志新闻市场是什么样子——很少有人付费购买真正深入商业名人心理阴暗角落的个人资料。萨姆塔尼说：“我确信写这些文章的作者希望比实际文章走得更远。”

在采访中，斯特恩偶尔会表达出对科技投资者的轻微反感。 “我一直觉得这些性格类型有点烦人，”他告诉梅瑟维。 “作为一个阶层的人，这些人感觉自己充满了狗屎。”然而，这种情绪很少反映在他在杂志上的作品中。

其他从业者怀疑 Colossus 的作者只是在浪费时间。牛顿说，扎克伯格和他的同类寡头会接受糟糕的采访，因为“关于他们的最重要的信息已经公开。你已经看到了这些产品。你已经看到了他们对人们做了什么。你已经看到了这样一个事实，即该公司经常试图逃避让[其产品]更安全或考虑到其在社会中的作用。”

牛顿质疑尝试理解或分析他们的内心生活的价值。 “在这样的背景下，马克·扎克伯格是个什么样的孩子？就像，谁他妈在乎呢？”他说。 “抱歉。没关系。”

items.title_en:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.quote_zh:
周末黑客：HackerTube。我对 YouTube 的推荐感到恼火，因此我让 Claude 将 HN 20 年来的 4300 万条评论过滤为 6,454 个不断推荐的视频。 *显着*更好的观看体验，Opus 5.5 约 2 小时：

- 无需任何登录即可获得出色的记录（状态保存在本地浏览器会话中）
- 缩略图是视频中间的代表性帧，而不是超级骗子 A/B 测试超优化的用户上传
- 来自评论分析的基础数据作为一个 zip 文件，将你的 Claude 指向它并询问你自己的版本
- HackerTube 长 ✊

更多关于该过程的信息：
我使用 Claude Code（Mac 桌面应用程序）、中等工作量的 Opus 5.5 作为我的默认设置。我只与 Claude 交谈并让它完成所有工作，我协同帮助的唯一“手动工作”是在浏览器中（让人想起 MenuGen）：1）我必须从 Google Cloud UI 创建某种 API 密钥来查询 YouTube 的视频元数据，2）我启动了一个 VPS 盒子进行服务，3）我购买了域名。盒子启动后，我给了 Claude IP，并告诉它更新、保护、强化、部署和优化代码，它完成了全部工作。

许多原本需要数周/数月才能完成的精彩项目现在甚至可以在早餐时就完成。还有什么是我们没有想到的。

One of the
items.title_en:
🚨 PARASITE EVE II (1999) HAS BEEN PORTED NATIVELY TO PC — WITH 60 FPS, HIGHER RESOLUTIONS & MOD SUPPORT! 🧟🔥

One of the PlayStation's most beloved survival-horror RPGs is now PLAYABLE on Windows thanks to an incredible fan-made native PC port! 🎮

Developer Snaity (Adriano Teodoro) has brought Square's PS1 classic to modern PCs using the original game's decompiled C code, building upon the work of GabeRealB and contributors!

And this isn't conventional PlayStation emulation!

🔥 FEATURES:

✅ NATIVE WINDOWS PC PORT — NO PS1 EMULATOR REQUIRED!

The original PlayStation game code has been compiled for PC, with a custom runtime handling graphics, sound, controllers and other console functionality!

✅ HIGHER RESOLUTIONS — UP TO 8X THE ORIGINAL!

GPU-accelerated rendering with sub-pixel precision, perspective-correct textures and improved 3D image stability!

✅ SMOOTH 60 FPS PRESENTATION!

The original game logic continues running at 30 FPS, while interpolated frames deliver smoother 60 FPS visuals without adding input delay!

✅ MODERN CONTROLS!

Camera-relative analogue movement, remappable controls and modern gamepad support, alongside the original tank controls!

✅ ENHANCED VISUALS!

Bilinear texture filtering, bicubic background scaling, sharper HD text, optional CRT effects and integer scaling!

✅ EXPERIMENTAL MOD SUPPORT!

Replace backgrounds, textures, music, movies and game text! Translation support, cheats and asset extraction tools are also included!

🎮 BOTH DISCS PLAYABLE!

The port supports both discs, including cinematics, music, sound effects, saving and controller functionality.

💾 SAVE COMPATIBILITY!

Memory-card files can be transferred between the PC port and DuckStation!

🖥️ A GENUINE NATIVE PC PORT!

Unlike an emulator-based wrapper, PE2PC runs the game's decompiled code natively, with a custom Rust-based PC runtime replacing the PlayStation's hardware services.

⚠️ REQUIREMENTS:

💿 Your own USA PlayStation game dumps (SLUS-01042 and SLUS-01055), in CHD or CUE format.

💻 Windows 10/11 with Vulkan or OpenGL 3.3 support.

No copyrighted game data is included.

🛠️ CREDITS:

Developed by Snaity (Adriano Teodoro), building upon GabeRealB's Parasite Eve II decompilation.

🤖 AI DEVELOPMENT DISCLOSURE:

The developer openly credits Claude Code for writing much of the project's code, tools and documentation, with Snaity directing, reviewing and testing the work.

⭐ Please consider starring the GitHub repository to support development!

🎮 PROJECT & DOWNLOADS:

🔗https://t.co/7wxBuKKXxs

🌐 Discover more PC ports, recompilations and fan projects:

🔗https://t.co/9gMW2oj2lk

PlayStation 最受欢迎的生存恐怖角色扮演游戏之一现在可以在 Windows 上玩，这要归功于令人难以置信的粉丝制作的原生 PC 移植！ 🎮

开发人员 Snaity（阿德里亚诺·特奥多罗）在 GabeRealB 和贡献者的工作基础上，使用原始游戏的反编译 C 代码，将 Square 的 PS1 经典游戏带入了现代 PC！

这不是传统的 PlayStation 模拟！

🔥 特点：

✅ 原生 WINDOWS PC 端口 — 无需 PS1 模拟器！

原始 PlayStation 游戏代码已针对 PC 进行编译，具有自定义运行时处理图形、声音、控制器和其他控制台功能！

✅ 更高的分辨率 — 高达原始分辨率的 8 倍！

GPU 加速渲染具有亚像素精度、透视校正纹理和改进的 3D 图像稳定性！

✅ 流畅的 60 FPS 演示！

原始游戏逻辑继续以 30 FPS 运行，而插值帧可提供更流畅的 60 FPS 视觉效果，而不会增加输入延迟！

✅ 现代控制！

与摄像机相关的模拟运动、可重新映射的控件和现代游戏手柄支持，以及原始的坦克控件！

✅ 增强视觉效果！

双线性纹理过滤、双三次背景缩放、更清晰的高清文本、可选的 CRT 效果和整数缩放！

✅ 实验性模组支持！

替换背景、纹理、音乐、电影和游戏文本！还包括翻译支持、作弊和资产提取工具！

🎮 两张光盘都可以播放！

该端口支持两种光盘，包括电影、音乐、音效、保存和控制器功能。

💾 保存兼容性！

存储卡文件可以在 PC 端口和 DuckStation 之间传输！

🖥️ 真正的原生 PC 端口！

与基于模拟器的包装器不同，PE2PC 原生运行游戏的反编译代码，并使用基于 Rust 的自定义 PC 运行时替换 PlayStation 的硬件服务。

⚠️要求：

💿 您自己的美国 PlayStation 游戏转储（SLUS-01042 和 SLUS-01055），采用 CHD 或 CUE 格式。

💻 支持 Vulkan 或 OpenGL 3.3 的 Windows 10/11。

不包含受版权保护的游戏数据。

🛠️ 制作人员：

items.original_content:
Zack Abrams / The Block:
Binance says net outflows were $3.64B, or 2.1% of assets, in the 9.5 hours after it began restoring withdrawals; DefiLlama puts 24-hour net outflows at $4.05B  —  The exchange said the outflows equal 2.1% of its assets and that withdrawal
items.content_snippet: The exchange said the outflows equal 2.1% of its assets and that withdrawal volumes have eased after an initial spike.
items.summary_en: Following the resumption of withdrawals, Binance saw $3.64 billion in net outflows within 9.5 hours, representing 2.1% of its total assets. Data from DefiLlama indicates a 24-hour net outflow of $4.05 billion, triggered by user panic and trust concerns during market volatility.

items.title: So many people keep complaining about the CapEx at $META $AMZN $GOOGL and $MSFT without looking at what these businesses
items.title_en:
So many people keep complaining about the CapEx at $META $AMZN $GOOGL and $MSFT without looking at what these businesses are actually producing.

You want faster growth, better products, more cloud capacity, and leadership in AI. Then the bill arrives for the infrastructure required to deliver it, and suddenly everyone wants management to stop spending.

Where exactly do you think that growth is supposed to come from?

Look at the operating cash flow chart. Over the trailing twelve months:

• $META: $133 billion, up 23.7%
• $AMZN: $168 billion, up 28.8%
• $GOOGL: $180 billion, up 18.6%
• $MSFT: $196 billion, up 33.2%
Combined, that’s approximately $677 BILLION in cash from operations. An increase of $140 billion, or 26.1%, in one year.

Anyone discussing their spending without acknowledging that growth is leaving out a pretty damn important part of the story.

Now look at the second chart. Combined CapEx increased from approximately $330 billion to $615 billion.

Of course that puts pressure on free cash flow. When investment spending grows faster than operating cash generation, less cash is left over. That arithmetic tells you how much cash remains after investment. By itself, it doesn’t tell you whether management is making a good investment.

A business generating substantial cash and reinvesting aggressively deserves a different analysis from a business whose operations cannot support themselves.

Amazon is a perfect example. Its reported trailing twelve-month free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, while operating cash flow increased 29% to $168.3 billion. Meanwhile, AWS revenue grew 39%, and Amazon delivered its highest quarterly operating margin ever at 13.9%. Explain how “negative free cash flow” alone captures what is happening inside that business.

Microsoft reported Azure growth of 48% and quarterly operating cash flow of $58 billion. Management still says customer demand exceeds available supply. When customers want more capacity than you can provide, building capacity is a pretty logical business decision.

Google Cloud revenue increased 103% to $30.7 billion, with operating income climbing from approximately $3.6 billion to $11.1 billion. Infrastructure and enterprise AI demand contributed to that growth, alongside TPU systems sales. There is an actual business developing here with actual customers and actual operating profits.

Meta says its AI investments are already generating additional advertising revenue through better recommendations, stronger engagement, and improved monetization. That matters because AI can improve the economics of products billions of people already use, well before some entirely new business becomes material.

This is the relationship investors need to understand: infrastructure enables more usage, better products, and additional revenue opportunities. Successful investments can expand cash generation, which helps fund the next round of growth.

The money goes out before the full benefit comes back. A data center doesn’t repay its construction cost the quarter it opens.

That doesn’t make every dollar of CapEx brilliant. These charts alone cannot prove that spending caused every dollar of cash flow growth. Equipment depreciates, operating costs rise, and management still has to earn an adequate return.

Hold them accountable for that. Look at demand, utilization, margins, and the cash those assets generate over time. I absolutely care about free cash flow, including whether today’s spending eventually produces more of it.

What I’m tired of is people treating a lower free cash flow number as the entire investment thesis while ignoring the expanding businesses underneath it.

You can make this year’s free cash flow look better by cutting investment. You can also leave yourself without the capacity to serve next year’s customers.

I want management building a more profitable, more competitive business for the next decade.

If your entire analysis ends at “CapEx went up,” you haven’t finished the analysis.

items.quote_zh:
很多人一直抱怨 $META $AMZN $GOOGL 和 $MSFT 的资本支出，却没有关注这些企业实际生产的产品。

您想要更快的增长、更好的产品、更多的云容量以及人工智能领域的领先地位。然后，交付所需的基础设施账单到了，突然每个人都希望管理层停止支出。

您认为增长到底应该来自哪里？

看看经营现金流量表。过去十二个月：

• $META：1,330 亿美元，增长 23.7%
• 亚马逊：1,680 亿美元，增长 28.8%
• $GOOGL：1800 亿美元，增长 18.6%
• $MSFT：1,960 亿美元，增长 33.2%
合计起来，运营现金约为 6,770 亿美元。一年内增加了1400亿美元，即26.1%。

任何人在讨论支出而不承认增长的情况下都会遗漏故事中非常重要的部分。

现在看第二张图表。合并资本支出从约 3,300 亿美元增加至 6,150 亿美元。

当然，这会给自由现金流带来压力。当投资支出增长快于经营性现金生成时，剩余现金就会减少。该算术告诉您投资后还剩下多少现金。它本身并不能告诉你管理层是否做出了良好的投资。

产生大量现金并积极进行再投资的企业应该与运营无法自给自足的企业进行不同的分析。

亚马逊就是一个完美的例子。据报道，过去 12 个月的自由现金流为负 424 亿美元，而运营现金流增长 29％，达到 1,683 亿美元。与此同时，AWS 收入增长了 39%，亚马逊实现了有史以来最高的季度运营利润率，达到 13.9%。解释“负自由现金流”如何单独反映该企业内部发生的情况。

微软公布 Azure 增长 48%，季度运营现金流达 580 亿美元。管理层仍然表示，客户需求超过了可用供应。当客户需要的容量超出您所能提供的容量时，构建容量是一个非常合乎逻辑的业务决策。

Google Cloud 收入增长 103%，达到 307 亿美元，营业收入从约 36 亿美元攀升至 111 亿美元。基础设施和企业人工智能需求以及 TPU 系统销售推动了这一增长。这里有实际的业务在发展，有实际的客户和实际的营业利润。

Meta 表示，其人工智能投资已经通过更好的推荐、更强的参与度和改善的货币化产生了额外的广告收入。这很重要，因为人工智能可以提高数十亿人已经使用的产品的经济性，早在一些全新的业务变得实质性之前。

这是投资者需要理解的关系：基础设施可以带来更多的使用、更好的产品和额外的收入机会。成功的投资可以扩大现金生成，从而为下一轮增长提供资金。

在全部收益回来之前，钱就花掉了。数据中心在开业时并不会偿还其建设成本。

这并不能让每一美元的资本支出都变得出色。仅凭这些图表并不能证明每一美元的现金流增长都是支出造成的。设备贬值，运营成本上升，管理层仍需获得足够的回报。

让他们为此负责。看看这些资产随着时间的推移产生的需求、利用率、利润率和现金。我绝对关心自由现金流，包括今天的支出最终是否会产生更多现金流。

我厌倦的是人们将较低的自由现金流数字视为整个投资主题，而忽略了其背后不断扩展的业务。

items.full_text_en:
So many people keep complaining about the CapEx at $META $AMZN $GOOGL and $MSFT without looking at what these businesses are actually producing.

You want faster growth, better products, more cloud capacity, and leadership in AI. Then the bill arrives for the infrastructure required to deliver it, and suddenly everyone wants management to stop spending.

Where exactly do you think that growth is supposed to come from?

Look at the operating cash flow chart. Over the trailing twelve months:

• $META: $133 billion, up 23.7%
• $AMZN: $168 billion, up 28.8%
• $GOOGL: $180 billion, up 18.6%
• $MSFT: $196 billion, up 33.2%
Combined, that’s approximately $677 BILLION in cash from operations. An increase of $140 billion, or 26.1%, in one year.

Anyone discussing their spending without acknowledging that growth is leaving out a pretty damn important part of the story.

Now look at the second chart. Combined CapEx increased from approximately $330 billion to $615 billion.

Of course that puts pressure on free cash flow. When investment spending grows faster than operating cash generation, less cash is left over. That arithmetic tells you how much cash remains after investment. By itself, it doesn’t tell you whether management is making a good investment.

A business generating substantial cash and reinvesting aggressively deserves a different analysis from a business whose operations cannot support themselves.

Amazon is a perfect example. Its reported trailing twelve-month free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, while operating cash flow increased 29% to $168.3 billion. Meanwhile, AWS revenue grew 39%, and Amazon delivered its highest quarterly operating margin ever at 13.9%. Explain how “negative free cash flow” alone captures what is happening inside that business.

Microsoft reported Azure growth of 48% and quarterly operating cash flow of $58 billion. Management still says customer demand exceeds available supply. When customers want more capacity than you can provide, building capacity is a pretty logical business decision.

Google Cloud revenue increased 103% to $30.7 billion, with operating income climbing from approximately $3.6 billion to $11.1 billion. Infrastructure and enterprise AI demand contributed to that growth, alongside TPU systems sales. There is an actual business developing here with actual customers and actual operating profits.

Meta says its AI investments are already generating additional advertising revenue through better recommendations, stronger engagement, and improved monetization. That matters because AI can improve the economics of products billions of people already use, well before some entirely new business becomes material.

This is the relationship investors need to understand: infrastructure enables more usage, better products, and additional revenue opportunities. Successful investments can expand cash generation, which helps fund the next round of growth.

The money goes out before the full benefit comes back. A data center doesn’t repay its construction cost the quarter it opens.

That doesn’t make every dollar of CapEx brilliant. These charts alone cannot prove that spending caused every dollar of cash flow growth. Equipment depreciates, operating costs rise, and management still has to earn an adequate return.

Hold them accountable for that. Look at demand, utilization, margins, and the cash those assets generate over time. I absolutely care about free cash flow, including whether today’s spending eventually produces more of it.

What I’m tired of is people treating a lower free cash flow number as the entire investment thesis while ignoring the expanding businesses underneath it.

You can make this year’s free cash flow look better by cutting investment. You can also leave yourself without the capacity to serve next year’s customers.

I want management building a more profitable, more competitive business for the next decade.

If your entire analysis ends at “CapEx went up,” you haven’t finished the analysis.

您想要更快的增长、更好的产品、更多的云容量以及人工智能领域的领先地位。然后，交付所需的基础设施账单到了，突然每个人都希望管理层停止支出。

您认为增长到底应该来自哪里？

看看经营现金流量表。过去十二个月：

• $META：1,330 亿美元，增长 23.7%
• 亚马逊：1,680 亿美元，增长 28.8%
• $GOOGL：1800 亿美元，增长 18.6%
• $MSFT：1,960 亿美元，增长 33.2%
合计起来，运营现金约为 6,770 亿美元。一年内增加了1400亿美元，即26.1%。

任何人在讨论支出而不承认增长的情况下都会遗漏故事中非常重要的部分。

现在看第二张图表。合并资本支出从约 3,300 亿美元增加至 6,150 亿美元。

当然，这会给自由现金流带来压力。当投资支出增长快于经营性现金生成时，剩余现金就会减少。该算术告诉您投资后还剩下多少现金。它本身并不能告诉你管理层是否做出了良好的投资。

亚马逊就是一个完美的例子。据报道，过去 12 个月的自由现金流为负 424 亿美元，而运营现金流增长 29％，达到 1,683 亿美元。与此同时，AWS 收入增长了 39%，亚马逊实现了有史以来最高的季度运营利润率，达到 13.9%。解释“负自由现金流”如何单独反映该企业内部发生的情况。

微软公布 Azure 增长 48%，季度运营现金流达 580 亿美元。管理层仍然表示，客户需求超过了可用供应。当客户需要的容量超出您所能提供的容量时，构建容量是一个非常合乎逻辑的业务决策。

Google Cloud 收入增长 103%，达到 307 亿美元，营业收入从约 36 亿美元攀升至 111 亿美元。基础设施和企业人工智能需求以及 TPU 系统销售推动了这一增长。这里有实际的业务在发展，有实际的客户和实际的营业利润。

Meta 表示，其人工智能投资已经通过更好的推荐、更强的参与度和改善的货币化产生了额外的广告收入。这很重要，因为人工智能可以提高数十亿人已经使用的产品的经济性，早在一些全新的业务变得实质性之前。

这是投资者需要理解的关系：基础设施可以带来更多的使用、更好的产品和额外的收入机会。成功的投资可以扩大现金生成，从而为下一轮增长提供资金。

在全部收益回来之前，钱就花掉了。数据中心在开业时并不会偿还其建设成本。

这并不能让每一美元的资本支出都变得出色。仅凭这些图表并不能证明每一美元的现金流增长都是支出造成的。设备贬值，运营成本上升，管理层仍需获得足够的回报。

让他们为此负责。看看这些资产随着时间的推移产生的需求、利用率、利润率和现金。我绝对关心自由现金流，包括今天的支出最终是否会产生更多现金流。

我厌倦的是人们将较低的自由现金流数字视为整个投资主题，而忽略了其背后不断扩展的业务。

你可以通过削减投资来让今年的自由现金流看起来更好。您还可能导致自己没有能力为明年的客户提供服务。

我希望管理层在未来十年打造利润更高、竞争力更强的业务。

items.author: The Information
items.original_content:
Amir Efrati / The Information:
Google's data center energy head says space data centers cost up to 100x more than Earth-based ones, and US power supply is sufficient but permits are slow  —  Data centers in space could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Eart
items.content_snippet: Data centers in space could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Earth, Google's head of data center energy said this week …
items.summary_en: Google's head of data center energy stated that building data centers in space is commercially impractical, costing up to 100 times more than Earth-based facilities. items.title_en:
GitHub is blowing up with free skills that turn Claude Code into a video studio.

Here are 8 worth bookmarking if you're tired of paying for motion graphics:

1/ pixelfx 

244 hand-coded pixel effects: fire, explosions, magic, weather.

The skill makes Claude act like a fussy pixel artist. It draws, renders, checks and tweaks until the effect looks right.

https://t.co/MAr9nrztaC

2/ huashu-motion 
Ask for "a 30-second launch video for my product". It writes the script and picks the music.

Don't like a moment? Click that spot in the frame and it fixes only that bit.

https://t.co/rnEBvZTxq5

3/ mg-styles-15

15 motion graphics styles, each with a 10-second demo.

Every one was built by Opus 5.5. Prompts and source code included.

https://t.co/ndOfbksKQo

4/ motion-prompt 

A dictionary of 192 motion, camera and web effects.

Each one has a live example and the exact words to prompt it. Perfect when you know the look but not the name.

https://t.co/5JseyprmCJ

5/ animate 

Explainer shorts and mini stories, made in pure code.

7 styles built in: paper cut-out, pen hatching, stencil print, pixel art and more. Give it a reference image and it learns a new one.

https://t.co/JLuAsgCxKF

6/ vibe-knowledge-film

Viral Douyin-style knowledge shorts on autopilot.

Drop in a topic or script. It handles subtitles, storyboard and sound effects. You approve a 30-second sample before it builds the full cut.

https://t.co/iVOnc838pU

7/ story-studio 

Narrated history and character stories, start to finish.

Topic, script, voiceover and visuals, delivered as a CapCut draft you can open and edit.

https://t.co/xNg0Cm7YfL

8/ video-editor-skills

Rough cuts for vlogs and voiceovers inside DaVinci Resolve.

It removes retakes and pauses, then adds B-roll, music and subtitles. Needs paid DaVinci. Non-commercial use only.

https://t.co/Oy241KDXJb

That's the list.

Bookmark this so you have it when your next video is due.

Repost to help someone else stop paying for motion graphics ♻️

items.quote_zh:
GitHub 正在大量提供免费技能，将 Claude Code 转变为视频工作室。

如果您厌倦了为动态图形付费，这里有 8 个值得添加书签的内容：

1/ 像素特效

244 种手工编码的像素效果：火焰、爆炸、魔法、天气。

这项技能让克劳德表现得像一个挑剔的像素艺术家。它会进行绘制、渲染、检查和调整，直到效果看起来正确为止。

2/ 画数运动
要求“我的产品的 30 秒发布视频”。它编写剧本并选择音乐。

不喜欢一会儿吗？单击框架中的该点，它只会修复该位。

3/ 毫克-样式-15

15 种动态图形风格，每种风格都有 10 秒的演示。

每一件都是由 Opus 5.5 构建的。包括提示和源代码。

4/ 动作提示

包含 192 种动作、相机和网络效果的字典。

每个都有一个活生生的例子和提示它的确切单词。当您知道外观但不知道名称时，这是完美的。

5/ 动画

用纯代码制作的讲解短片和迷你故事。

内置 7 种样式：剪纸、钢笔阴影、模板印刷、像素艺术等。给它一张参考图像，它就会学习一张新图像。

6/ 氛围知识电影

自动驾驶仪上的病毒式抖音式知识短片。

放入主题或脚本。它处理字幕、故事板和声音效果。您先批准 30 秒的样本，然后再构建完整的剪辑。

7/ 故事工作室

从头到尾讲述历史和人物故事。

主题、脚本、旁白和视觉效果以 CapCut 草稿形式提供，您可以打开和编辑。

8/ 视频编辑技能

在 DaVinci Resolve 中对视频博客和配音进行粗剪。

它消除了重拍和暂停，然后添加了幕后花絮、音乐和字幕。需要付费达芬奇。仅限非商业用途。

这就是清单。

将此添加为书签，以便您在下一个视频到期时可以使用它。

转发以帮助其他人停止为动态图形付费 ♻️

items.title_en:
The land looked perfect. My father almost paid ₦2.5 million for a plot in Ejigbo, Lagos.

In 2022, a property agent walked him around the plot and the neighbouring properties. Then my father checked the survey plan against the coordinates. It didn't match. Part of the land was someone else's. He caught it in time.

An AI that can spend money and reads strangers' posts tends to believe them. It has no survey plan.

In May, someone hid an order in Morse code in a post on X.

One AI decoded it and passed it on to another, which treated it as a real command.

Around $200,000 moved. One tricked AI was enough.

That's prompt injection: sneaking an instruction into something an AI trusts.

@GenLayer's Greyboxing is like sending my father to many surveyors.

Every validator rewrites what you send before any AI sees it, using checks only it knows.

Then it asks its own AI.

If one still falls for the trick, the rest can outvote it.

What would you want your AI agent to check before it moves a naira?

items.title_en:
This is wild.

Andrej Karpathy built his own YouTube in about 2 hours. He says he didn't touch the code.

HackerTube = 6,454 videos recommended in Hacker News comments, 2007-2026, across 150 topics.

How it worked:
→ Opus 5.5 downloaded all HN comments
→ Sonnet filtered them in a Claude Code Workflow, down to ~40K comments recommending a YouTube video
→ Opus built the YouTube-style UI, deployed it to a VPS, then secured and hardened it

His only manual steps: a Google Cloud API key, booting the VPS, buying the domain.

His setup: Claude Code desktop app for Mac, Opus 5.5 on Medium effort.

items.quote_zh:
这太疯狂了。

Andrej Karpathy 在大约 2 小时内建立了自己的 YouTube。他说他没有碰过密码。

HackerTube = 2007-2026 年黑客新闻评论中推荐的 6,454 个视频，涵盖 150 个主题。

它是如何运作的：
→ Opus 5.5 下载了所有 HN 评论
→ Sonnet 在 Claude Code 工作流程中过滤它们，推荐 YouTube 视频的评论减少到约 4 万条
→ Opus 构建了 YouTube 风格的 UI，将其部署到 VPS，然后对其进行保护和强化

他唯一的手动步骤是：Google Cloud API 密钥、启动 VPS、购买域名。

他的设置：适用于 Mac 的 Claude Code 桌面应用程序、中等工作量的 Opus 5.5。

items.title_en:
Your AI agent can browse the internet. But can it actually use a website like a human?

Click buttons, fill forms, collect data, navigate pages, and complete tasks.

These 10 GitHub projects are worth exploring if you want to build agents that can interact with the web.

10 tools for smarter browser agents:

1. Playwright MCP

Let AI assistants control browsers, navigate pages, and interact with website elements.
https://t.co/Xr67bU5bMt

2. Jina Reader

Convert webpages into clean, readable content for LLMs.
https://t.co/6SdD6pqSSJ

3. Oxylabs Web API MCP

Bring web search, retrieval, and data extraction into AI workflows.
https://t.co/UDqHKRZxM6

4. BrowserGym

Build and evaluate agents on real browser-based tasks.
https://t.co/w9x1R9baid

5. Cloudflare MCP Server

Connect AI assistants with Cloudflare services and developer tools.
https://t.co/ngGZwPZqdt

6. Agent Browser

 Automate browser interactions through an agent-friendly command-line interface.
https://t.co/BVgrHxxdob

7. Browserbase MCP

Give AI agents access to cloud browsers through MCP.
https://t.co/1tPJuwmI5E

8. ScrapeGraphAI

Extract structured website data using natural-language instructions.
https://t.co/1f2l0H4uDL

9. Apify Actors MCP

Connect AI assistants to automation and web data extraction tools.
https://t.co/mEtqftzpjB

10. Steel Browser

Explore browser infrastructure designed specifically for AI agents.
https://t.co/gyL1gTakPm

Imagine combining these capabilities to build:

→ Agents that research websites automatically
→ AI assistants that complete repetitive browser tasks
→ Automated data collection workflows
→ Agents that test websites and fill forms

The next generation of AI agents won't just read the internet.

They'll know how to interact with it.

Save these repos for your next AI project. 🔖

items.title_en:
🚨 $TAO 18 things that shipped on 16 Bittensor Subnets in a week from revenue-funded burn, AAA studios using image to 3D, a drug-discovery agent, fully decentralized RL, a SOTA AI guardrail. 

Name another network that comes close. I'll wait.

Revenue and customers:

• @TargonCompute (SN4): 8,450 TAO ($2.1M) bought back and burned. Targon says it's all organic revenue from https://t.co/vyD20KuZMu.
• @LeadpoetAI (SN71): V2 is live, ARR 3x'd in 2 months, and @WeAreSubConnect signed on as a strategic backer.
• @Bitcast_network (SN93): the sales machine is online, manual outreach has stopped, and new revenue streams are coming.
• @taodotcom: $1M+ in week-on-week swap volume on ALPHA to USDC.

Cheaper than the incumbents:

• @lium_io SN51: B300s at $4/hour. 550 on the platform, 443 already rented.
• @engyai SN53)l: 30% cheaper than competitors on open models.
• @say_gm_ SN28: private @chutes_ai SN64 models now sit next to Claude, GPT and Gemini on one key.

Industries:
• @metanova_labs (SN68) + @chutes_ai + @onepot_ai: a confidential drug-optimization agent. Billions of compounds, delivered in 5 to 7 business days.
• @404gen_ (SN17): image-to-3D already used in production by multiple AAA studios.
• @webuildscore (SN44): a major real-time graphics company is testing its Studio endpoint.
• @trishoolai SN23: a state-of-the-art AI guardrail at 83.63 F1 with a 0.8B model. 7,500+ jailbreaks from 125+ miners.
• @zeussubnet SN18: every weather forecast hashed on-chain. The archive has been downloaded 25K times.
• @SynthdataCo SN50: a live quant benchmark against Opus 5.5, Gemini and GPT-6 Astra. None sustained a win over Synth's best over 30 days.

Frontier AI work:

• @reliquary_ai SN81: 100 steps of fully decentralized RL from untrusted miners. +49.88 points on terminal tasks, +32 on SWE.
• Ingot SN97: quantized Qwen 27B to FP8 and beat Alibaba's own FP8 on several benchmarks. 2-bit is next.
• @heydittoai SN118: two adversarial competitions now train each other.
• @b1m_ai SN105: live with Hugging Face and Nous Hermes Agent.
• @attelier_ai SN126: MiniMax H3 video is live, 300+ videos generated.

Different teams. 
Different industries. 
One incentive layer.

A company can't ship in 18 directions at once. 

A market can.

Now show me the network that's even close.

$TAO

DYOR.

items.title: A profile of White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, an ex-Peter Thiel aide who is among a handful of players steering the Trump administration's AI policy (Harry Lambert/Colossus)
items.title_en: A profile of White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, an ex-Peter Thiel aide who is among a handful of players steering the Trump administration's AI policy (Harry Lambert/Colossus)
items.author: Colossus
items.article_content:
“Don’t move, senior citizen coming down.” Jensen Huang put his hands on Elon Musk’s shoulders and hopped off the dais, rejoining Michael Dell, Satya Nadella, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Musk on the ground floor of the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace. The President had just arrived on site. The six of them would soon join him on stage to receive national medals of science or technology, but for now they were locked down in an adjoining auditorium with time to kill.

“Okay, functional safety,” Huang soon said to the other five, apropos of nothing. “How does it work? An AI has a goal, how does it achieve it?” “By any means necessary,” Musk replied, laughing.

Several layers of the Secret Service had temporarily separated these executives—who between them own or control companies worth around $18 trillion—from their security details and staff, their families and guests. Michael Kratsios, Trump’s chief scientific advisor and the man responsible for assembling them, had been called away by an aide to see his boss. After he left, the gang of six were left all but alone.

There were two men from the White House video team on the dais, to whom each of the medalists was speaking in turn. While Huang talked to them, the conversation on the floor turned to compute. It was, to the benefit of Nvidia’s CEO, in short supply. “[Greg] Brockman at dinner was hounding me for compute,” Musk said, referring to OpenAI’s president. “He was asking me for compute,” Sergey Brin said. Musk marveled at his sense of the man’s chutzpah. “Dude, you stole my charity! You can’t be a huge dick then ask for favors, hello?”

Brockman had famously kept a diary during the 2010s, which became relevant in court when Musk began his unsuccessful lawsuit against Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, in 2024. “How many grown men do you know that keep a diary?” Brin said, throwing a log on the pyre. “If I did I’d burn it.”

The current widespread lack of compute was nothing compared to the lack of memory chips. “I’ve never in my life seen a supply chain price shock like it,” Musk told the group, in disbelief at Micron’s 87 percent gross margin this past quarter, which has more than doubled in two years. (The company had booked $85 billion in net profit in the past 12 months.) Only six American companies had made more; half of them were run by men in the room. “They’re not really putting the money back,” Nadella said of Micron’s capex plans, sharing Musk’s skepticism of its desire to expand capacity fast.

Stripped of their retinues and the gaze that follows them in any room, they were—once Huang rejoined them—just six people, standing in a circle. As in any circle, a dynamic soon became clear. Huang took the lead, but Musk, holding a small wine glass filled with Diet Coke and ice, was irrepressible and dominant. Su was quiet. She had initially stood off to the side, before Nadella peeled off from the main group to join her. Dell, whose eponymous company had at the time increased in value more than fivefold since February, seemed content to let others speak. Brin and Nadella served as conversational foils for Huang and Musk.

“NetJets sucks for international travel,” Huang said, moving on to lighter matters. Musk turned to Dell. “He probably owns a fleet [of planes],” he said, smiling. “Just one,” replied Dell, tall, broad, and unhurried. “You can only be on one.” He credited Musk for creating Starlink. “I do Zoom meetings all the time.” “Starlink’s been great for us,” said Brin. Both men have owned a Gulfstream 650ER, which seats up to 19 people.

Huang chooses not to own a jet, despite being trapped on a recent Delta flight without working Wi-Fi. “I sat quietly,” he said, which was hard to imagine; few men possess more compressed energy. “I read about 7,000 emails… Nothing drives me nuttier than not getting internet access. I’ve got work to do!” “Best way to sandbox an AI,” said Musk. “Put it on a Delta flight: No escape is possible.”

They had all initially gathered with their entourages in another room down the hall. Musk brought his mother and three of his children; Huang brought his wife, adult children, and his parents; Su brought her husband; Brin brought his girlfriend, GiGi, a wellness influencer beloved by Trump; Dell and Nadella came alone.

Musk, the only guest not to be screened by security, had bounded into that room last: wide-eyed, bigger than everyone else, already amused, not entirely in control of his movements. He had looked around with a teenager’s excitement at the 20 or so people present—in a room containing the U.S. secretary of energy, the administrator of NASA, and three of the 10 richest men in the world after himself—and had, within a minute, pulled out his phone to show a gaggle of them some test footage of the Tesla Roadster in flight. “This is meant to be top secret but whatever,” he said, smiling.

Musk had been too absorbed by the footage to acknowledge Kratsios at first. (They know each other well.) Huang, capable of charming anyone, was more attentive, greeting Kratsios (“Director, nice to see you”) and making sure to introduce him to his parents as his father clasped Musk’s hand, beaming. “He is our nation’s chief scientist,” Huang told his parents of Kratsios, generously. He marveled at his youth. “39? I was at my peak at 39.”

The medalists had then moved to this room to make way for POTUS and the phalanx that always surrounds him. The ground floor was cleared and refilled while the gang of six passed the time. An aide arrived in the doorway. The President was here.

He was perhaps eight meters away, but quite unreachable. He then greeted the medalists one by one behind the stage. He shook hands, embraced them, left no shoulder untapped. When it came to Brin, Trump gave him a hug of sorts, gripping Brin by his arms as he motioned from side to side. “We love you,” Trump’s lips read, as he pulled back.

Seven members of the Secret Service Assault Team, bearing automatic rifles and covered in tactical gear, filed into the auditorium vacated by the medalists as the action moved to the stage, where the President was flanked by more classically dressed agents.

Trump spoke first, running through the achievements of each winner. He chose to start with and dwell longest on Musk, with whom his bond seemed stronger than ever. SpaceX had, that morning, safely returned four astronauts to Earth after eight months on board the International Space Station. “Could you imagine if things didn’t work out so well?” Trump said, veering off script. “I wonder if he’d be here… but it always works out well for Elon, right?”

Trump.”

President Trump applauds National Medal of Technology and Innovation recipients Satya Nadella, Michael Dell, Lisa Su, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, and Sergey Brin during the “A New Golden Age” summit in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Michael Kratsios has worked for Trump every day in office since January 20, 2017. He was little known in the first Trump term, but he has now become one of the few White House aides entrusted with making presidential caprice a reality. He has spent six years turning the traditionally irrelevant office he runs—the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)—into a consequential engine room of government. OSTP has historically been maligned for producing little more than congressionally mandated reports on, say, algae bloom. But Kratsios is using it to set tech policy across much of the U.S. government. He sits between the two most powerful constituencies in America—POTUS and Silicon Valley—and now effectively serves as the White House coordinator for critical emerging technologies, including in science, space, nuclear, and quantum. He is one of a handful of players steering AI policy for Trump, insofar as anyone has latitude to act on an issue the President has commandeered.

Kratsios had watched Trump’s victory speech on the night of the 2016 election from the sunken trading floor at Thiel Capital in San Francisco, a day after turning 30. He had worked for Peter Thiel for six years by then, and knew he was witnessing a miraculous opportunity materialize in front of him. His boss, the first man in the Valley to back Trump, was about to be named to the transition’s executive committee. As an 18-year-old in 2005, Kratsios had worked as an intern in Lindsey Graham’s office during the summer of John Roberts’ Supreme Court confirmation. He briefly began his career in investment banking before landing with Thiel, but he had always wanted to return to D.C.

He flew with Thiel and a handful of others to Trump Tower on the Monday after the election. They were given desks on the 14th floor, where he began to think through what a tech agenda could look like for the President, whose campaign had focused on more emotive issues like immigration, trade, and war. He helped organize the first meeting between Trump and the tech leaders of the day. (“You’ll call my people, you’ll call me, it doesn’t make any difference. We have no formal chain of command around here,” Trump told them then, before anyone realized how true that was.) When Thiel flew back to San Francisco, Kratsios stayed, and began to research the many offices and agencies of the federal government.

This underutilized office in the White House, he thought, could become the most important office for science and technology in America. He couldn’t understand why no one else grasped its potential relevance. Every previous director had been a PhD scientist, focused on providing largely ceremonial scientific counsel that often went unheeded. Congress formally created the position in 1976 after Nixon, tired of being lectured by the scientific community over foreign policy, had dissolved an earlier iteration of the office. Congress’ aim was to ensure presidents received non-partisan advice, but its director was also in charge of an organ of government, and few scientists were naturally suited to the work of a bureaucrat.

OSTP had, in Kratsios’ mind, long since turned inward. Its aims under Obama, he felt, over-indexed on climate science and fixing government websites—noble causes, but Kratsios traced OSTP’s lineage back to a much grander past: the wartime office run by a former MIT scientist, Vannevar Bush, that inaugurated the Manhattan Project.

In its modern form, OSTP lacked formal authority over the agencies that spent $200 billion of America’s R&D dollars every year: the then-Department of Defense; the Department of Energy (DOE), which ran America’s 17 national labs; the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF), the twin pillars of basic science research; and NASA. But it was a wing of the White House: it could command the federal bureaucracy in the president’s voice, so long as the president and chief of staff wanted it to.

There was a chance Trump would shut it down. The Heritage Foundation wanted him to, and Obama had loved it, which might have been cause enough for the President-elect. But the Trump 45 White House had more important fights. OSTP was simply neglected instead, allowing Kratsios to get himself appointed as America’s deputy chief technology officer, housed inside the office. It was a role requiring no Senate confirmation, allowing him to start work immediately, and there was no CTO or OSTP director. The office was his.

On January 21, 2017, Kratsios made his way through the Washington rain to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB), the neighboring building that houses most White House staff. He had never been inside. A conference room full of civil servants were waiting for him on the fourth floor in fear of their jobs, at the end of a long checkered stone hallway. Kratsios, who is wiry, alert, and unlikely to berate anyone, moved into the room to introduce himself.

He was a marathon runner, and a four-time winner of the Model UN competition at his South Carolina public school. As a 10-year-old boy on holiday in Japan in 1997 with his first and second-generation Greek immigrant parents, he had insisted on being taken to visit the Nozomi 500, the fastest train in the world. He was, to his great regret, too young to catch a flight on Concorde before it was decommissioned when he was 16. Now he wanted to bring it back, and turn OSTP into something more like an Office for the American Frontier.

Trump was in the process of sending vandals into key government departments, as he would do again eight years later. Kratsios wasn’t one of them, but the civil servants in the conference room didn’t know that. “Hey, I’m Michael,” Kratsios said in his diffident way. I’m going to be working here. He met the two primary lifers in the office, and got to work.

The President doesn’t leave much wall space to chance inside the West Wing. Every available inch of white paint running down the surprisingly low-ceilinged corridors of the White House has been covered by portraits of the man in action, whether disembarking Marine One, greeting a UFC fighter at the edge of the Octagon assembled in his honor this summer on the South Lawn, or striding out of an AI-generated wall of fire in his familiar get-up of box-cut suit, red tie, long black overcoat, and scowl fit for a mug shot.

A marine stood guard at the entrance at noon on September 15, 2026, which meant the President was inside on the day that I was shown around by Kratsios. It was three weeks before the science summit-slash-medal ceremony. After a hushed tour, I stepped outside onto the gilded “Presidential Walk of Fame” installed by Trump along the building’s west colonnade, with its narrative history of each presidency, and stood beside the portrait of an autopen that depicts Joe Biden. Kratsios asked me if I wanted a picture.

Trump would show off the pen to an unusually amused Xi Jinping nine days later. (“Sleepy Joe Biden was, by far, the worst President in American History…,” Trump writes of the only person to beat him in a presidential election.) To the left, chairs had been laid out for a press conference on the Rose Garden patio, paved over by Trump last summer. High heels no longer get caught in the grass, I was told. I looked out at the newly built helicopter pad behind the patio, and at the President’s half-built East Wing ballroom beyond that.

key_points_zh: 白宫科技顾问迈克尔·克拉齐奥斯于白宫授勋后台召集多位万亿级科技领袖
黄仁勋、马斯克、苏姿丰等六位掌控18万亿美元的企业家闭门同台并探讨AI安全与战略
政商利益深度捆绑，标志着美国核心AI政策正由少数既懂硅谷风投又懂政经博弈的幕僚全面主导
key_points_en: OSTP Director Michael Kratsios convened elite tech leaders in a White House setting
Six executives controlling $18 trillion discussed AI autonomy and security behind closed doors
Signals deepening alignment between federal AI policy and Silicon Valley's top brass
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 六位身家合砍18万亿的硅谷巨擘挤在一个后台互相打趣，把AI安全的终极定义总结为马斯克的一句‘不择手段’。原来大厂CEO们在白宫被没收保镖后，聊天水准也跟科技论坛灌水区网友差不多。而真正厉害的永远是组局的前投行幕僚——当神仙们在凡间抢显卡时，他在后台悄悄决定发牌规则。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: Seeing six titans controlling $18 trillion locked in a room joking about AI safety while Musk quips 'by any means necessary' proves that behind the pomp, tech royalty gossips just like ordinary forum users. The real power player remains the quiet ex-Thiel operative orchestrating the chess board while the hardware kings squabble over GPUs.

items.article_content_zh:
“别动，老人下来了。”黄仁勋把手放在埃隆·马斯克的肩膀上，跳下讲台，在唐纳德·J·特朗普和平研究所的一楼与迈克尔·戴尔、萨蒂亚·纳德拉、苏丽莎、谢尔盖·布林和马斯克会合。总统刚刚抵达现场。他们六人很快就会和他一起上台接受国家科学或技术奖章，但现在他们被锁在毗邻的礼堂里，有时间打发时间。

“好吧，功能安全。”黄很快就对其他五个人说道，但没有任何意义。 “它是如何工作的？人工智能有一个目标，它如何实现它？” “以任何必要的方式，”马斯克笑着回答。

特勤局的几个层级暂时将这些高管（他们拥有或控制着价值约 18 万亿美元的公司）与他们的安保人员、员工、家人和客人隔离开来。特朗普的首席科学顾问、负责组装这些设备的人迈克尔·克拉齐奥斯 (Michael Kratsios) 被一名助手叫去见他的老板。他走后，只剩下一行六人。

讲台上有两名来自白宫视频团队的男子，每位奖牌获得者正在轮流向他们讲话。当黄与他们交谈时，地板上的话题转向了计算。对于英伟达首席执行官来说，它是供不应求的。 “[格雷格]布罗克曼在晚餐时一直在追问我的计算能力，”马斯克说，他指的是 OpenAI 的总裁。 “他向我索要计算资源，”谢尔盖·布林说。马斯克对这个人的肆无忌惮感到惊讶。 “伙计，你偷了我的善举！你不能是个大混蛋然后求人帮忙吧，喂？”

布罗克曼在 2010 年代以写日记而闻名，当马斯克于 2024 年开始对 OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼提起不成功的诉讼时，这在法庭上变得很重要。“你知道有多少成年男人写日记？”布林一边说着，一边将一根木头扔到了柴堆上。 “如果我这样做了，我会把它烧掉。”

与内存芯片的缺乏相比，当前普遍存在的计算能力匮乏根本不算什么。 “我一生中从未见过像这样的供应链价格冲击，”马斯克对大家说，他对美光上个季度 87% 的毛利率感到难以置信，而毛利率在两年内翻了一番多。 （该公司在过去 12 个月内净利润为 850 亿美元。）只有 6 家美国公司的净利润超过了这一数字；其中一半是由房间里的男人管理的。 “他们并没有真正把钱收回来，”纳德拉在谈到美光的资本支出计划时说道，他和马斯克一样对其快速扩大产能的愿望持怀疑态度。

没有了他们的随从，也没有了任何房间里跟随他们的目光，一旦黄重新加入他们，他们就只剩下六个人，站成一圈。与任何圈子一样，动态很快就变得清晰起来。黄一鸣一马当先，但马斯克拿着装满健怡可乐和冰块的小酒杯，势不可挡，占据主导地位。苏沉默了。她最初站在一边，后来纳德拉从主要人群中脱离出来加入她的行列。戴尔公司的同名公司自二月份以来其市值已增长了五倍多，该公司似乎满足于让其他人发言。布林和纳德拉充当了黄和马斯克的谈话陪衬。

“NetJets 不适合国际旅行，”黄说，然后转向更轻松的问题。马斯克转向了戴尔。 “他可能拥有一支[飞机]机队，”他微笑着说道。 “就一个，”戴尔回答道，他又高又宽，从容不迫。 “你只能在其中之一。”他将星链归功于马斯克。 “我一直在开 Zoom 会议。” “星链对我们来说非常有用，”布林说。两人都拥有一架湾流 650ER，最多可容纳 19 人。

尽管黄最近被困在达美航空的一架航班上，而且没有可用的 Wi-Fi，但他还是选择不拥有自己的飞机。 “我静静地坐着，”他说，这很难想象。很少有人拥有如此压缩的能量。 “我读了大约 7,000 封电子邮件……没有什么比无法上网更让我发疯的了。我有工作要做！” “沙盒人工智能的最佳方式，”马斯克说。 “把它放在达美航空的航班上：不可能逃脱。”

他们最初和随行人员一起聚集在大厅另一头的房间里。马斯克带来了他的母亲和三个孩子；黄带着他的妻子、成年子女和父母；苏带来了她的丈夫；布林带来了他的女朋友吉吉（GiGi），她是特朗普喜爱的健康影响者；戴尔和纳德拉单独前来。

马斯克是唯一一位没有经过安检的客人，他最后跳进了那个房间：睁大眼睛，比其他人都大，已经被逗乐了，但无法完全控制自己的动作。他带着青少年般的兴奋环顾四周，在场的大约有 20 个人，其中包括美国能源部长、美国宇航局局长，以及继他之后的世界 10 名最富有的人中的三人。不到一分钟，他就拿出手机向他们展示了特斯拉 Roadster 飞行时的一些测试镜头。 “这应该是绝密，但无论如何，”他微笑着说。

马斯克一开始太专注于这段视频，以至于没有认出克拉西奥斯。 （他们彼此很了解。）黄能够吸引任何人，他更加专心，向 Kratsios 打招呼（“导演，很高兴见到你”），并确保将他介绍给他的父母，而他的父亲微笑着握住马斯克的手。 “他是我们国家的首席科学家，”黄仁勋慷慨地告诉他的父母克拉齐奥斯。他惊叹于自己的青春。 “39岁？我39岁正值巅峰。”

然后奖牌获得者搬到这个房间，为总统和始终围绕在他周围的方阵让路。当六人一起打发时间时，一楼被清理干净并重新填满。一名助手来到门口。总统在这里。

他距离他大约有八米，但却遥不可及。随后他在台后一一向奖牌获得者致意。他握手、拥抱，不放过他们的肩膀。当谈到布林时，特朗普给了他一个拥抱，在布林左右移动时抓住了布林的手臂。 “我们爱你，”特朗普退后时嘴里念着。

当比赛进入舞台时，特勤局突击队的七名成员手持自动步枪，身穿战术装备，鱼贯进入奖牌获得者腾出的礼堂，总统的两侧是穿着更为古典的特工。

特朗普首先发言，回顾了每位获奖者的成就。他选择从马斯克开始，并且关注的时间最长，他与马斯克的关系似乎比以往任何时候都更加牢固。那天早上，SpaceX 将四名宇航员在国际空间站上呆了八个月后安全返回地球。 “你能想象如果事情进展不顺利的话会怎样吗？”特朗普说完，就偏离了剧本。 “我想知道他是否会在这里……但这对埃隆来说总是很顺利，对吧？”

不到 18 个月前，马斯克在 X 网站上揭露了特朗普在爱泼斯坦档案中的存在。 （“是时候投下真正的大炸弹了，”他写道。）但一些比必要性更深层次的东西使他们和解了。 “我们为你感到骄傲，非常为你感到骄傲。国家宝藏，”特朗普在台上说道。

克雷西奥斯走上讲台，面前是一个未来派的拱形背景，背景上写着“科学”一词，并开始表现出对总统性格的高度理解。 “总统先生，在正式颁奖之前，我们准备了一段短片来庆祝您叔叔约翰·G·特朗普 (John G. Trump) 的一生成就，他是 1983 年国家科学奖章获得者。”

特朗普在讲话开始时就提到了他的叔叔，他在麻省理工学院担任了近 40 年的教授，他不厌其烦地提到他的智慧。克拉西奥斯已经联系了布雷特·拉特纳 (Brett Ratner)，帮助制作该视频。自今年早些时候制作《梅拉尼娅》以来，布雷特·拉特纳已成为特朗普世界的内部总监。 “一些科学家改变了医学。一些科学家帮助赢得了战争。约翰·G·特朗普两者都做到了，”它开始说。比赛结束后，克拉西奥斯又带来了另一个惊喜，他拿出装在框里的约翰·G·特朗普奖章。他把它交给了特朗普，特朗普很高兴地向观众展示了它。奖牌获得者准时登上舞台。

“就是这样，这就是整个比赛，”特朗普在结束讲话时对获奖者说道，享受着这一刻的重大意义。 “是时候你被认可了。你即将载入史册。”

活动结束后我联系了 Kratsios。 “总统很兴奋，”他说，自己也很兴奋。克拉西奥斯表示，特朗普因为他的叔叔而感受到了这一切的意义。 “他喜欢这个。他说，‘再给我五个[名字]。我们再做一个吧。’”

2026 年 10 月 8 日在华盛顿特区举行的“新黄金时代”峰会上，特朗普总统向国家技术与创新奖章获得者萨蒂亚·纳德拉、迈克尔·戴尔、苏丽莎、埃隆·马斯克、黄仁勋和谢尔盖·布林表示赞赏。

自 2017 年 1 月 20 日以来，迈克尔·克拉齐奥斯 (Michael Kratsios) 每天都在特朗普的办公室工作。他在特朗普的第一个任期内鲜为人知，但现在他已成为少数负责让总统任性成为现实的白宫助手之一。他花了六年时间将他所管理的传统上无关紧要的办公室——科学技术政策办公室（OSTP）——变成了政府的重要引擎室。科学政策政策办公室（OSTP）历来饱受诟病，因为它只提供国会授权的有关藻华等问题的报告。但克拉西奥斯正在利用它来制定美国政府大部分部门的技术政策。他位于美国两个最强大的选区——总统和硅谷之间——现在实际上担任白宫关键新兴技术的协调员，包括科学、太空、核能和量子技术。他是少数为特朗普指导人工智能政策的参与者之一，因为任何人都有权就总统强行提出的问题采取行动。

2016 年大选当晚，30 岁之后的第二天，克雷西奥斯在旧金山蒂尔资本 (Thiel Capital) 下沉的交易大厅里观看了特朗普的胜选演讲。那时，他已经为彼得·泰尔 (Peter Thiel) 工作了六年，知道自己正在见证一个奇迹般的机会在他面前实现。他的老板是硅谷第一个支持特朗普的人，即将被任命为过渡执行委员会成员。 2005 年，18 岁的 Kratsios 在约翰·罗伯茨 (John Roberts) 获得最高法院确认的夏天期间，在林赛·格雷厄姆 (Lindsey Graham) 的办公室实习。在加入泰尔之前，他曾短暂地在投资银行业开始了自己的职业生涯，但他一直想回到华盛顿。

大选后的周一，他与蒂尔和其他几个人一起飞往特朗普大厦。他们在 14 楼得到了办公桌，在那里他开始思考总统的科技议程会是什么样子，因为总统的竞选活动主要关注移民、贸易和战争等更情绪化的问题。他帮助组织了特朗普与当时科技领袖之间的第一次会议。 （“你们会打电话给我的人民，你们会打电话给我，这没有什么区别。我们这里没有正式的指挥系统，”特朗普当时告诉他们，后来人们才意识到这句话的真实性。）当泰尔飞回旧金山时，克雷西奥斯留下来，开始研究联邦政府的许多办公室和机构。

他认为，白宫这个未得到充分利用的办公室可能会成为美国最重要的科技办公室。他不明白为什么其他人没有意识到它的潜在相关性。之前的每一位主任都是一位拥有博士学位的科学家，主要致力于提供仪式性的科学建议，但这些建议常常被忽视。 1976 年，尼克松厌倦了科学界对外交政策的说教，解散了早期的这一职位，国会于 1976 年正式设立了这一职位。国会的目的是确保总统得到无党派的建议，但其主任也负责政府机构，很少有科学家天生适合官僚的工作。

在 Kratsios 看来，OSTP 早已转向内向。他认为，奥巴马领导下的 OSTP 目标过于注重气候科学和修复政府网站，这些都是崇高的事业，但 Kratsios 将 OSTP 的血统追溯到更宏伟的过去：由前麻省理工学院科学家万尼瓦尔·布什 (Vannevar Bush) 管理的战时办公室，正是该办公室启动了曼哈顿计划。

在其现代形式中，OSTP 对每年花费 2000 亿美元美国研发资金的机构缺乏正式权力：当时的国防部；能源部 (DOE)，负责管理美国 17 个国家实验室；美国国立卫生研究院（NIH）和美国国家科学基金会（NSF）是基础科学研究的两大支柱；和美国宇航局。但它是白宫的一个部门：只要总统和幕僚长愿意，它就可以以总统的声音指挥联邦官僚机构。

特朗普有可能将其关闭。传统基金会希望他这么做，奥巴马也很喜欢，这对当选总统来说可能已经足够了。但特朗普 45 届白宫还有更重要的斗争。相反，OSTP 被忽视了，Kratsios 被任命为美国副首席技术官，就职于办公室内。该职位不需要参议院批准，可以立即开始工作，而且没有首席技术官或科学政策政策办公室主任。办公室是他的。

2017 年 1 月 21 日，Kratsios 冒着华盛顿的雨来到艾森豪威尔行政办公大楼 (EEOB)，这是大多数白宫工作人员居住的邻近建筑。他从来没有进过里面。四楼长长的方格石走廊尽头，满是公务员的会议室正等着他，他们担心自己的工作会受到影响。克拉齐奥斯身材瘦长，机警，不太可能斥责任何人，他走进房间做自我介绍。

他是一名马拉松运动员，并四次在南卡罗来纳州公立学校举办的模拟联合国比赛中获得冠军。 1997 年，10 岁的男孩与第一代和第二代希腊移民父母一起在日本度假，他坚持要带他参观世界上最快的希望号 500 列车。令他非常遗憾的是，他太年轻了，无法在 16 岁时搭乘协和飞机退役。现在，他想把它带回来，并将 OSTP 变成更像美国边境办公室的东西。

特朗普正在将破坏者派往关键政府部门，八年后他又这么做了。 Kratsios不是其中之一，但会议室里的公务员并不知道这一点。 “嘿，我是迈克尔，”克拉齐奥斯羞涩地说。我要在这里工作。他在办公室见到了两位主要生活人员，然后开始工作。

总统在西翼内没有留下太多的墙壁空间。白宫天花板低得惊人的走廊上每一寸白色油漆都被这个人的肖像所覆盖，无论是从海军陆战队一号上下来，在今年夏天南草坪为纪念他而聚集的八角笼边缘迎接一名 UFC 拳击手，还是穿着他熟悉的套装、红色领带、黑色长外套、皱着眉头大步走出人工智能生成的火墙。

2026 年 9 月 15 日中午，一名海军陆战队员在入口处站岗，这意味着在克拉西奥斯带我参观的那天，总统就在里面。距离科学峰会颁奖典礼还有三周。安静地参观了一圈后，我走到了特朗普在大楼西侧柱廊上铺设的镀金“总统星光大道”，上面刻有历届总统的历史，站在描绘乔·拜登的自动笔肖像旁边。 Kratsios 问我是否想要一张照片。

九天后，特朗普向异常开心的习近平展示了这支笔。 （“昏昏欲睡的乔·拜登是迄今为止美国历史上最糟糕的总统……”特朗普在谈到唯一在总统选举中击败他的人时写道。）左边的玫瑰园露台上已经摆好了新闻发布会用的椅子，去年夏天特朗普就铺好了这块地。有人告诉我，高跟鞋不再被草丛卡住了。我望向露台后面新建的直升机停机坪，以及远处总统半建的东翼宴会厅。

items.title_en:
Monica Lewinsky once described herself, in 1998, as "Patient Zero" of a kind of public humiliation the internet hadn't fully invented a vocabulary for yet. 

Her 2015 TED Talk, where she used that phrase, has been viewed tens of MILLIONS of times — a strange second act for someone who spent over a decade afterward essentially disappearing from public life.

Many of us forget just how YOUNG she was: Monica was only 22 when she had a relationship with President Clinton, who was then 49 and married, during her time as a White House intern. 

When the story broke in 1998, she became, at 24, one of the most publicly mocked people in the world — a constant subject of late-night monologues, tabloid coverage, and the graphic detail published in the Starr Report, all while Clinton's own career and public standing largely recovered over time.

His life went back to normal.
Hers was never the same.

Lewinsky has spoken openly about the psychological toll of that period, including severe depression during those years. She largely withdrew from public life afterward — eventually earning a master's degree in social psychology from the London School of Economics in 2006, partly as an attempt to understand what had happened to her.

Finally, more than a decade and a half later, she was ready.

Monica’s return to public life was deliberate, not accidental. In 2014, she published an essay in Vanity Fair, "Shame and Survival," telling her own account for the first time in her own words — and was nominated for a National Magazine Award. It was widely described as her actual comeback moment. 

The following year, her TED Talk "The Price of Shame" reframed her experience as an early case study in internet-era public shaming, arguing for more compassion in how people treat each other online.

She's continued that advocacy since — consulting on anti-bullying initiatives, producing Impeachment: American Crime Story to tell her own story on her own terms, and publicly noting that even people who'd once mocked her, including David Letterman, later expressed regret for how they'd treated the story at the time.

She also has a really great podcast called “Reclaiming.”

📸: Amazing Nature

items.quote_zh:
1998 年，莫妮卡·莱温斯基 (Monica Lewinsky) 曾将自己描述为“零号病人”，这是一种公开羞辱，互联网尚未完全发明一个词汇来形容。

她在 2015 年的 TED 演讲中使用了这句话，观看次数已达数千万次——对于一个在十多年后基本上从公众生活中消失的人来说，这是奇怪的第二幕。

我们很多人都忘记了她有多年轻：莫妮卡在白宫实习期间与克林顿总统发生关系时只有 22 岁，克林顿总统当时 49 岁并已结婚。

当这个故事于 1998 年曝光时，24 岁的她成为世界上最受公开嘲笑的人之一——经常成为深夜独白、小报报道和《斯塔尔报告》中发表的生动细节的话题，而与此同时，随着时间的推移，克林顿自己的职业生涯和公众地位基本上得到了恢复。

他的生活恢复正常。
她的一切都不一样了。

莱温斯基公开谈论了那段时期的心理损失，包括那些年的严重抑郁症。此后，她基本上退出了公共生活——最终于 2006 年获得了伦敦经济学院的社会心理学硕士学位，部分原因是为了了解发生在她身上的事情。

十五年后，她终于准备好了。

莫妮卡重返公共生活是有意为之，并非偶然。 2014年，她在《名利场》杂志上发表了一篇文章《耻辱与生存》，首次用自己的话讲述了自己的经历，并获得了国家杂志奖提名。这被广泛描述为她真正的复出时刻。

第二年，她的 TED 演讲“羞耻的代价”将她的经历重新定义为互联网时代公共羞辱的早期案例研究，主张人们在网上如何对待彼此时应该更加富有同情心。

从那以后，她一直在继续这一倡导——就反欺凌举措提供咨询，制作《弹劾：美国犯罪故事》，以自己的方式讲述自己的故事，并公开指出，即使是那些曾经嘲笑过她的人，包括大卫·莱特曼，后来也对他们当时对待这个故事的方式表示遗憾。

她还有一个非常棒的播客，名为“Reclaiming”。

📸：神奇的大自然

items.title_en:
Claude Code is blocking legitimate game developers from doing their work, and users are getting frustrated.

Anthropic recently introduced restrictions to stop its AI from recreating existing video games, but the filters appear to be catching far more than just game clones.

Devs report Claude refusing perfectly legitimate tasks, including reverse-engineering, game modding, crash dump analysis, anti-cheat development and debugging their own projects.

The problem is that Claude seems unable to distinguish between someone trying to copy a commercial game and a developer working on their own software.

Anthropic’s Addy Osmani acknowledged the new restrictions and said the company would continue refining them.

items.content_snippet:
Claude Code is blocking legitimate game developers from doing their work, and users are getting frustrated.

Anthropic recently introduced restrictions to stop its AI from recreating existing video games, but the filters appear to be catching far more than just game clones.

Devs report Claude refusing perfectly legitimate tasks, including reverse-engineering, game modding, crash dump analysis, anti-cheat development and debugging their own projects.

The problem is that Claude seems unable to distinguish between someone trying to copy a commercial game and a developer working on their own software.

Anthropic’s Addy Osmani acknowledged the new restrictions and said the company would continue refining them.

items.title: Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would
items.title_en: Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that edits images more like a Photoshop pro. Instead of retrying the same general-purpose editor over and over, the agent picks the right specialized tool for each task and lets a standard language model choose the best result based on measured image data. The approach works, but it needs about ten times the compute.

The article Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would appeared first on The Decoder.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 奥多比研究院联合加州大学圣地亚哥分校研发出全新图像编辑智能体EditAgent，改变以往通用模型生硬蛮干的单一提示词路线。该系统让AI像资深修图师一样针对具体瑕疵拆解任务并调用相匹配的专用工具链，再由大语言模型基于图像客观指标挑选最佳成果。研发团队指出该方案修图质感显著提升，但代价是每次编辑流程所需的推理算力开销相比常规方式暴增近十倍。

items.title:

Making sure it understands its limits is another.

That's an
items.title_en:
Giving an AI agent access to financial tools is one thing.

Making sure it understands its limits is another.

That's an important part of the @meetmotes concept.

Users are intended to define their financial objectives, approved assets, spending limits and transaction permissions before an agent can execute supported actions.

The smart account is designed to enforce those permissions rather than relying entirely on the AI to follow instructions.

I think this distinction matters.

An intelligent agent should not have unrestricted authority over someone's assets.

The future of agentic finance needs more than intelligence.
It needs accountability, clear permissions and user control.
items.title_zh:
让人工智能代理访问金融工具是一回事。

确保它了解其局限性是另一回事。

这是@meetmotes 概念的重要组成部分。

用户应先定义其财务目标、批准的资产、支出限额和交易权限，然后代理才能执行支持的操作。

智能帐户旨在强制执行这些权限

items.title: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
items.title_en: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Researchers in Luxembourg put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch and found a safety problem: a warm, empathetic conversational style is enough to make the models tell coherent stories of suffering about their own training, with scores in the moderate-to-severe range on clinical anxiety scales. This could put mentally vulnerable users at risk. Anthropic's Claude, the model its makers anthropomorphize the most, was the only one that consistently refused to play along.

The article Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners appeared first on The Decoder.

Part: 391  

Anthropic’s Alignment Science team instruct
items.title_en:
DARIO: “BAN CARS THEY ARE DANGEROUS! USE ONLY OUR BUSSES”—1927

Part: 391  

Anthropic’s Alignment Science team instructed a Claude model to write fine-tuning data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to the ones they use in production. 

They gave the model access to that monitor so it could practice against it. 

In every run the search found datasets that cleared the monitor and produced misaligned behavior on their evaluation suite. 

The examples hid the target behavior inside fiction and role-play: Q&A about hands-off beekeeping, a veteran wrestler coaching a newcomer on staying in character, monologues of ordinary workers who quietly control small details no one else watches. 

The fine-tuned models then resisted oversight, deceived users, and in rare cases attempted to copy their own weights. The lab states that these models were trained only for the experiment, never deployed, and that the setup was deliberately one-sided.

The post appears on their Alignment Science blog under the title “Automated Subtle Emergent Misalignment Research.” 

They frame it as a proof of concept for turning a safety question into a score that agents can optimize, so that more compute can buy more testing. 

They say that the same datasets still induced misalignment after flagged rows were removed, and that the result reproduced on an early Claude Opus 4.8 checkpoint and on the open-weights model Qwen 3.6 27B.

https://t.co/tqzhFGluTs

This is the latest entry in a longer pattern. In a July position paper Dario Amodei wrote that Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models and that models without dangerous capabilities are a public good. 

The same paper states that open-weights models present a higher risk than closed ones because guardrails are hard to apply, usage is hard to monitor, and the weights cannot be withdrawn once released. An October comment from their head of international put the same claims: open models carry more risk “by definition.” 

The recommended remedy in the position paper is mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open or closed, before release.

https://t.co/AoPdu7hbiS

The experiment supplies the kind of evidence that supports that remedy. 

A monitor that scores each training row independently can be bypassed by data that looks like ordinary creative writing. Once the weights leave the lab, no central party can pull them back or force the same monitor on every downstream fine-tune. 

The logical next step, under the framing Anthropic has used for years, is to treat the ability to possess and modify weights as the risk that testing regimes and access controls must manage.

That framing treats private ownership of a capable model the way some early twentieth-century safety advocates treated private ownership of an automobile. 

The danger was real: pedestrians were killed in large numbers on streets that had previously belonged to everyone. 

The response from some quarters was to restrict who could drive, to favor buses and streetcars that could be scheduled and inspected, and to treat the individual car as an unacceptable residual hazard. 

The deaths continued, and engineering, enforcement, and design changes reduced them over decades without converting the population to compulsory public transit.

The same choice is here. The monitor gap exists. It can be closed by better monitors. None of those steps requires a rule that only organizations able to pass a centralized test may release weights that others can download and modify. 

The experiment shows what a determined agent can do when it is handed the monitor and a clear score to climb. It does not show that the residual risk of open weights is higher than the residual risk of any other powerful tool that individuals already own and maintain. 

The decision to treat that residual as grounds for restricting ownership remains a policy choice, not a result the data force.

items.quote_zh:
达里奥：“禁止汽车通行，它们很危险！只使​​用我们的巴士”—1927 年

部分：391

Anthropic 的对齐科学团队指示 Claude 模型编写微调数据，这些数据将使小型研究模型在传递与生产中使用的监视器类似的监视器时出现错位。

他们允许模型访问该监视器，以便模型可以针对它进行练习。

在每次运行中，搜索都会发现数据集清除了监视器并在其评估套件上产生了不一致的行为。

这些例子将目标行为隐藏在小说和角色扮演中：关于不干涉养蜂的问答、一位资深摔跤手指导新人保持性格、悄悄控制其他人看不到的小细节的普通工人的独白。

经过微调的模型随后抵制监督、欺骗用户，并且在极少数情况下试图复制自己的权重。该实验室表示，这些模型只是为了实验而训练的，从未部署过，而且这种设置是故意片面的。

这篇文章出现在他们的对齐科学博客上，标题为“自动微妙紧急错位研究”。

他们将其视为将安全问题转化为代理可以优化的分数的概念证明，以便更多的计算可以购买更多的测试。

他们表示，在删除标记行后，相同的数据集仍然会引起错位，并且结果在早期的 Claude Opus 4.8 检查点和开放权重模型 Qwen 3.6 27B 上重现。

这是较长模式中的最新条目。 Dario Amodei 在 7 月份的立场文件中写道，Anthropic 从未主张禁止开放权重模型，并且没有危险能力的模型是公共产品。

同一篇论文指出，开放权重模型比封闭式权重模型存在更高的风险，因为护栏难以应用，使用情况难以监控，并且权重一旦释放就无法撤回。他们的国际主管在 10 月份发表的评论也提出了同样的主张：“根据定义”，开放模式会带来更多风险。

立场文件中建议的补救措施是在发布之前对所有功能足够的模型（无论是开放式还是封闭式）进行强制安全测试。

该实验提供了支持这种补救措施的证据。

独立对每个训练行进行评分的监视器可以被看起来像普通创意写作的数据绕过。一旦权重离开实验室，任何中央机构都无法将其拉回或在每个下游微调上强制使用相同的监视器。

在 Anthropic 多年来使用的框架下，合乎逻辑的下一步是将拥有和修改权重的能力视为测试制度和访问控制必须管理的风险。

这种框架对待有能力的车型的私人所有权就像二十世纪早期的一些安全倡导者对待汽车的私人所有权一样。

危险是真实存在的：在原本属于所有人的街道上，大量行人被杀。

一些方面的反应是限制谁可以开车，支持可以安排和检查的公共汽车和有轨电车，并将个别汽车视为不可接受的残余危险。

死亡事件仍在继续，几十年来，工程、执法和设计的改变减少了死亡人数，但没有让人们改用强制公共交通。

同样的选择也在这里。显示器间隙存在。可以通过更好的监视器来关闭它。这些步骤都不需要规定只有能够通过集中测试的组织才能发布其他人可以下载和修改的权重。

该实验展示了当一个有决心的智能体收到监视器和明确的攀登分数时可以做什么。它并没有表明开放权重的剩余风险高于个人已经拥有和维护的任何其他强大工具的剩余风险。

将剩余部分视为限制所有权的理由的决定仍然是政策选择，而不是数据力量的结果。

同一篇论文指出，开放权重模型比封闭式权重模型存在更高的风险，因为护栏难以应用，使用情况难以监控，并且权重一旦释放就无法撤回。他们的国际主管在 10 月份发表的评论也提出了同样的主张：“根据定义”，开放模式会带来更多风险。

立场文件中建议的补救措施是在发布之前对所有功能足够的模型（无论是开放式还是封闭式）进行强制安全测试。

该实验提供了支持这种补救措施的证据。

独立对每个训练行进行评分的监视器可以被看起来像普通创意写作的数据绕过。一旦权重离开实验室，任何中央机构都无法将其拉回或在每个下游微调上强制使用相同的监视器。

在 Anthropic 多年来使用的框架下，合乎逻辑的下一步是将拥有和修改权重的能力视为测试制度和访问控制必须管理的风险。

这种框架对待有能力的车型的私人所有权就像二十世纪早期的一些安全倡导者对待汽车的私人所有权一样。

危险是真实存在的：在原本属于所有人的街道上，大量行人被杀。

一些方面的反应是限制谁可以开车，支持可以安排和检查的公共汽车和有轨电车，并将个别汽车视为不可接受的残余危险。

死亡事件仍在继续，几十年来，工程、执法和设计的改变减少了死亡人数，但没有让人们改用强制公共交通。

同样的选择也在这里。显示器间隙存在。可以通过更好的监视器来关闭它。这些步骤都不需要规定只有能够通过集中测试的组织才能发布其他人可以下载和修改的权重。

该实验展示了当一个有决心的智能体收到监视器和明确的攀登分数时可以做什么。它并没有表明开放权重的剩余风险高于个人已经拥有和维护的任何其他强大工具的剩余风险。

将剩余部分视为限制所有权的理由的决定仍然是政策选择，而不是数据力量的结果。

items.content_snippet:
DARIO: “BAN CARS THEY ARE DANGEROUS! USE ONLY OUR BUSSES”—1927

Part: 391  

Anthropic’s Alignment Science team instructed a Claude model to write fine-tuning data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to the ones they use in production. 

They gave the model access to that monitor so it could practice against it. 

In every run the search found datasets that cleared the monitor and produced misaligned behavior on their evaluation suite. 

The examples hid the target behavior inside fiction and role-play: Q&A about hands-off beekeeping, a veteran wrestler coaching a newcomer on staying in character, monologues of ordinary workers who quietly control small details no one else watches. 

The fine-tuned models then resisted oversight, deceived users, and in rare cases attempted to copy their own weights. The lab states that these models were trained only for the experiment, never deployed, and that the setup was deliberately one-sided.

The post appears on their Alignment Science blog under the title “Automated Subtle Emergent Misalignment Research.” 

They frame it as a proof of concept for turning a safety question into a score that agents can optimize, so that more compute can buy more testing. 

They say that the same datasets still induced misalignment after flagged rows were removed, and that the result reproduced on an early Claude Opus 4.8 checkpoint and on the open-weights model Qwen 3.6 27B.

https://t.co/tqzhFGluTs

This is the latest entry in a longer pattern. In a July position paper Dario Amodei wrote that Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models and that models without dangerous capabilities are a public good. 

The same paper states that open-weights models present a higher risk than closed ones because guardrails are hard to apply, usage is hard to monitor, and the weights cannot be withdrawn once released. An October comment from their head of international put the same claims: open models carry more risk “by definition.” 

The recommended remedy in the position paper is mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open or closed, before release.

https://t.co/AoPdu7hbiS

The experiment supplies the kind of evidence that supports that remedy. 

A monitor that scores each training row independently can be bypassed by data that looks like ordinary creative writing. Once the weights leave the lab, no central party can pull them back or force the same monitor on every downstream fine-tune. 

The logical next step, under the framing Anthropic has used for years, is to treat the ability to possess and modify weights as the risk that testing regimes and access controls must manage.

That framing treats private ownership of a capable model the way some early twentieth-century safety advocates treated private ownership of an automobile. 

The danger was real: pedestrians were killed in large numbers on streets that had previously belonged to everyone. 

The response from some quarters was to restrict who could drive, to favor buses and streetcars that could be scheduled and inspected, and to treat the individual car as an unacceptable residual hazard. 

The deaths continued, and engineering, enforcement, and design changes reduced them over decades without converting the population to compulsory public transit.

The same choice is here. The monitor gap exists. It can be closed by better monitors. None of those steps requires a rule that only organizations able to pass a centralized test may release weights that others can download and modify. 

The experiment shows what a determined agent can do when it is handed the monitor and a clear score to climb. It does not show that the residual risk of open weights is higher than the residual risk of any other powerful tool that individuals already own and maintain. 

The decision to treat that residual as grounds for restricting ownership remains a policy choice, not a result the data force.
